@us/acs-3/59588.purpose: NASA's Advanced Composite Solar Sail System, a 12U CubeSat built with NanoAvionics and run jointly by NASA Ames and NASA Langley Research Center. It deployed four seven-metre composite booms that tension roughly 80 square metres of aluminised polymer sail across four quadrants, testing whether lightweight composite boom structures can scale to practical solar sailing. The sail deployed successfully in August 2024. It is a propulsion technology demonstrator, not an operational science mission.

@us/aepex/68506.organization: NASA / LASP, University of Colorado Boulder
@us/aepex/68506.purpose: AEPEX — Atmospheric Effects of Precipitation through Energetic X-rays — is a 6U CubeSat built and operated by LASP at the University of Colorado Boulder under NASA's CubeSat Launch Initiative. Its AXIS instrument images the bremsstrahlung X-rays given off when radiation-belt electrons crash into the upper atmosphere, and from those it reconstructs the flux and energy spectrum of the incoming electrons. That precipitation is one of the main ways the radiation belts lose particles, and one of the least well measured. Launched March 2026 and collecting data.

@us/aerocube-16a/59290.purpose: A 6U CubeSat from The Aerospace Corporation, the non-profit federally funded research centre that flies most of the small experimental satellites the national-security space programme learns from. AeroCube-16 is a two-satellite Flashlight experiment: each carries a laser communications terminal under two kilograms that points with fast-steering mirrors rather than by slewing the whole spacecraft, aiming to hold an optical crosslink at 500 km separation. Both halves were released together on the NRO's NROL-123 Electron launch.

@us/aerocube-16b/59291.purpose: A 6U CubeSat from The Aerospace Corporation, the non-profit federally funded research centre that flies most of the small experimental satellites the national-security space programme learns from. AeroCube-16 is a two-satellite Flashlight experiment: each carries a laser communications terminal under two kilograms that points with fast-steering mirrors rather than by slewing the whole spacecraft, aiming to hold an optical crosslink at 500 km separation. This is the second half of the pair; the crosslink only means anything with both ends flying.

@us/aerocube-18a/63220.purpose: A 6U CubeSat from The Aerospace Corporation, one of a pair flying a mixed payload: a hyperspectral imaging unit, a set of nanotechnology experiments, and advanced solar cells whose output is trended over time. The five-year mission length is the point — the aim is not a single measurement but long-run performance data on how these parts degrade, which is what decides whether a technology is fit for an operational government mission. One of the pair released together on the Transporter-13 rideshare into a sun-synchronous orbit.

@us/aerocube-18b/63222.purpose: A 6U CubeSat from The Aerospace Corporation, one of a pair flying a mixed payload: a hyperspectral imaging unit, a set of nanotechnology experiments, and advanced solar cells whose output is trended over time. The five-year mission length is the point — the aim is not a single measurement but long-run performance data on how these parts degrade, which is what decides whether a technology is fit for an operational government mission. The second of the pair, released on the same Transporter-13 rideshare into a matching sun-synchronous orbit.

@us/aerocube-5c/40965.purpose: A 1.5U, roughly two-kilogram CubeSat from The Aerospace Corporation's PicoSat programme. The AeroCube-5 series existed to test on-orbit pointing and tracking from a spacecraft too small to carry conventional attitude hardware, which is the capability every optical or laser payload on a CubeSat depends on. 5C is the third of the series and the only one still flying: it launched separately from 5A and 5B, which went up in December 2013 and have since re-entered.

@us/aerocube-6a/40045.purpose: One of a pair of half-U CubeSats from The Aerospace Corporation carrying three microdosimeter variants each, measuring electrons from roughly 43 to 830 keV and protons from 370 keV to 12 MeV. The pair exists to separate space from time: flying two identical dosimeters at a controllable in-track separation shows whether a particle event seen at one spacecraft explains an anomaly at another. Operators steer that gap by differential drag, tilting one satellite off Sun-point with torque rods so it presents more area. 6A was deployed from the UniSat-6 host; its twin then separated from it.

@us/aerocube-6b/40046.purpose: One of a pair of half-U CubeSats from The Aerospace Corporation carrying three microdosimeter variants each, measuring electrons from roughly 43 to 830 keV and protons from 370 keV to 12 MeV. The pair exists to separate space from time: two identical dosimeters at a controllable in-track separation show whether a particle event seen at one spacecraft explains an anomaly at another. Operators steer that gap by differential drag. 6B separated from 6A after deployment, and its data are a public NASA heliophysics dataset.

@us/aerocube-7/40966.purpose: AeroCube-7A, flown as OCSD-A, the Optical Communications and Sensor Demonstration, built by The Aerospace Corporation under NASA's Small Spacecraft Technology Program. It carried a 6 W, 1064 nm downlink laser aimed at a 30 cm ground terminal, attempting 200 Mbit/s from a 1.5U CubeSat — roughly a hundred times the radio downlink typical of the class. It was a pathfinder and it partly failed: a software upload in August 2016 disabled attitude control, and without pointing there was no laser link. The follow-on OCSD-B and -C later succeeded.

@us/aerocube-8c/41853.purpose: One of the four AeroCube-8 spacecraft, mission name IMPACT, from The Aerospace Corporation. The headline payload is SiEPro, a scalable ion-electrospray propulsion system developed by MIT's Space Propulsion Laboratory — thrusters that extract ions directly from a liquid salt, with no gas, tanks or valves, giving a CubeSat real propulsion at a scale that had never flown before. Alongside it the satellite measures four- and five-junction solar cells, a carbon-nanotube wiring harness and carbon-nanotube radiation shielding. This one flew as a secondary payload on the WorldView-4 launch.

@us/aerocube-8d/41852.purpose: One of the four AeroCube-8 spacecraft, mission name IMPACT, from The Aerospace Corporation. The headline payload is SiEPro, a scalable ion-electrospray propulsion system developed by MIT's Space Propulsion Laboratory — thrusters that extract ions directly from a liquid salt, with no gas, tanks or valves, giving a CubeSat real propulsion at a scale that had never flown before. Alongside it the satellite measures four- and five-junction solar cells, a carbon-nanotube wiring harness and carbon-nanotube radiation shielding. This one flew as a secondary payload on the WorldView-4 launch.

@us/aggiesat6/68634.purpose: A 6U CubeSat built by Texas A&M University's AggieSat Lab and flown as Nanosat-10 under the Department of Defense University Nanosatellite Program. Its primary payload is a radio-frequency antenna array that detects transmissions from Iridium satellites and runs the MuSiC direction-finding algorithm onboard to derive bearing vectors and orbit estimates, a proof of concept for space-based space domain awareness. A dosimeter secondary payload measures the low-energy electron environment to refine LEO radiation models.

@us/alice/39467.organization: U.S. Air Force Institute of Technology
@us/alice/39467.purpose: ALICE — the AFIT LEO iMESA CNT Experiment — is a 3U CubeSat designed, built and operated by the US Air Force Institute of Technology at Wright-Patterson AFB, on a Pumpkin-built bus supplied through the National Reconnaissance Office's Colony-1 programme. It carries an Integrated Miniaturized Electrostatic Analyzer for in-situ plasma measurement together with a Georgia Tech carbon-nanotube array assessed as a small-satellite propulsion technology. It was AFIT's first satellite and flew inside the GEMSat/ELaNa-II secondary-payload container.

@us/amc-14/32708.organization: SES Americom -> U.S. Department of Defense
@us/amc-14/32708.purpose: A Lockheed Martin A2100AXS Ku-band direct-broadcast satellite built for SES Americom, with capacity contracted to EchoStar. A Proton-M/Briz-M upper-stage failure left it in a far too low transfer orbit and SES declared it a total loss. It was then sold to the U.S. Department of Defense, which raised it using the spacecraft's own thrusters until it reached geosynchronous altitude in January 2009. It operates from an inclined geosynchronous orbit rather than a fixed commercial slot.

@us/andesite/45726.organization: Boston University Center for Space Physics
@us/andesite/45726.purpose: A 6U CubeSat built and operated by the Boston University Center for Space Physics to resolve small-scale field-aligned currents in the aurora. The mule spacecraft carried several picosatellite nodes, each with its own three-axis magnetometer, power system and radio, intended to fly as a loose swarm only a few hundred metres apart and relay magnetic-field data back through the Globalstar network. It flew as a NASA ELaNa CubeSat Launch Initiative payload.

@us/anduril-216/69879.purpose: A 200 kg technology demonstrator operated by Anduril Industries and built on Apex Space's Aries bus. It carries electro-optical and long-wave infrared sensors and flies to validate detection and tracking of both ground scenes and other orbiting objects, giving geospatial awareness and space domain awareness from the same payload. The flight doubles as an on-orbit qualification of the Aries platform for advanced remote-sensing missions.

@us/ao-91/43017.purpose: RadFxSat, designated AMSAT-OSCAR 91 once in orbit: a 1U CubeSat flown by AMSAT-NA carrying a Vanderbilt University radiation-effects experiment that characterises how commercial semiconductor parts degrade in the space environment. Its amateur payload is a cross-band FM bent-pipe repeater, 70 cm uplink and 2 m downlink, still widely used by operators. Battery deterioration has left it working in sunlight only as a carrier-operated repeater, with the flight computer failed and no telemetry.

@us/ao-95/43770.purpose: Fox-1Cliff, a 1U amateur-radio cubesat built by AMSAT with university partners and flown on the SSO-A rideshare. It carries a mode U/V FM voice repeater plus a Vanderbilt radiation-effects experiment, a Virginia Tech camera and a Penn State-Erie MEMS gyro. Telemetry showed a healthy spacecraft, but commissioning found an anomaly in the receiver, and AMSAT announced that it would not be commissioned as an operational amateur satellite. It remains in orbit as a telemetry beacon rather than a usable repeater.

@us/apex-aries-1/59129.purpose: Aries SN1, flown under the mission name Call to Adventure, was the first flight of Apex Space's series-produced Aries satellite bus — an ESPA-class platform of roughly 200 kg wet mass that the Los Angeles company sells as an off-the-shelf product. It carried no single mission payload but a set of hosted customer experiments, including an onboard-compute board for Ubotica and payloads for major defence primes. The point of the flight was to qualify the bus itself.

@us/aprizesat-1/28372.purpose: A store-and-forward messaging microsatellite built by SpaceQuest of Fairfax, Virginia, flown originally as LatinSat C and later renumbered into the AprizeSat series. It carries no imager: it collects short data bursts from unattended remote terminals such as buoys, pipelines, containers and vehicles as it passes overhead, then replays them to a gateway on a later pass. This first pair predates the shipborne AIS receivers that were added from AprizeSat 3 onward.

@us/aprizesat-10/40019.purpose: The last of the AprizeSat line, catalogued commercially as exactView 13 and flown with AprizeSat 9. Like the rest of the AIS-equipped units it pairs a store-and-forward machine-to-machine relay with a VHF receiver tuned to ship AIS transmissions. Twelve-kilogram spacecraft of this class established the commercial maritime-domain-awareness data market that navies and coastguards now buy into rather than build.

@us/aprizesat-2/28366.purpose: The companion to AprizeSat 1 and the fourth of the original LatinSat batch, flown as LatinSat D. Built by SpaceQuest, it provides store-and-forward machine-to-machine messaging and asset tracking: the spacecraft acts as a delayed relay, buffering short bursts from remote ground terminals until it can dump them to a gateway. Like its twin it carries no AIS receiver, that payload arriving with the 2009 pair.

@us/aprizesat-3/35686.purpose: The first AprizeSat to carry a space-based AIS receiver, also catalogued as exactView 3. Alongside the store-and-forward data payload it listens for the VHF Automatic Identification System transmissions that ships broadcast, giving wide-area maritime traffic picture at sea beyond coastal receiver range. For a naval watchstander this is the commercial root of space-based maritime domain awareness, cooperative, unencrypted, and dependent on vessels choosing to transmit.

@us/aprizesat-4/35684.purpose: The second AIS-equipped AprizeSat, also designated exactView 4, launched with AprizeSat 3 and operated by SpaceQuest on behalf of COM DEV and later exactEarth. It combines the family's store-and-forward IoT messaging relay with a VHF AIS receiver for ship reporting. Flying the pair together gave the constellation two crossing opportunities per orbit plane, the first step toward the revisit rate that makes space AIS useful for tracking rather than spot-checking.

@us/aprizesat-5/37792.purpose: A SpaceQuest-built AprizeSat carrying both the store-and-forward data relay and a VHF AIS receiver, catalogued commercially as exactView 5. Space-based AIS reception is harder than it sounds: the satellite sees thousands of ships at once in a single beam and their self-organised time slots collide, so useful yield depends on receiver design and on repeated passes rather than a single look.

@us/aprizesat-6/37793.purpose: An AprizeSat flown with number 5 and carrying the same store-and-forward messaging payload plus a VHF AIS receiver; it appears in commercial records as exactView 6 and later as Myriota 2 after the Australian IoT operator Myriota acquired part of the fleet in 2020. The ownership trail is worth noting: the same physical spacecraft is sold under different brand names as the maritime and IoT data businesses change hands.

@us/aprizesat-7/39416.purpose: A SpaceQuest microsatellite catalogued commercially as exactView 5R, a replacement-generation unit in the AprizeSat line. It carries the family's store-and-forward machine-to-machine relay together with a VHF AIS receiver for ship position reporting. Small, cheap and long-lived, these spacecraft demonstrated that global maritime traffic reporting did not require a large dedicated satellite, only enough of them to cut the revisit interval.

@us/aprizesat-8/39425.purpose: An AprizeSat flown alongside number 7 and catalogued as exactView 12, carrying a VHF AIS receiver in addition to the store-and-forward data payload common to the series. AAC SpaceQuest has described the later AprizeSats as heavily tasked for AIS collection, each returning on the order of a million ship messages a day, which is the practical scale at which space AIS becomes a usable maritime picture rather than a sample.

@us/aprizesat-9/40018.purpose: A SpaceQuest-built AprizeSat catalogued as exactView 11 and later as Myriota 4, carrying the store-and-forward IoT relay and a VHF AIS receiver. Its role is unglamorous but persistent: buffering short telemetry bursts from unattended sensors and ship AIS transmissions on one pass and delivering them to a ground gateway on the next, with latency measured in tens of minutes rather than seconds.

@us/arcstone/64540.purpose: Arcstone is a 6U CubeSat carrying a hyperspectral instrument that measures sunlight reflected from the Moon between roughly 350 and 2300 nanometres. NASA Langley Research Center leads the mission and Blue Canyon Technologies operates the spacecraft. The aim is to pin lunar spectral reflectance down to well under one percent uncertainty, so the Moon can serve as a stable, free, universally visible calibration standard for other Earth-observing and remote-sensing instruments. It launched on the Transporter-14 rideshare in June 2025.

@us/arcturus/56371.purpose: Astranis Arcturus, the first of the company's MicroGEO satellites — a 300 kg geostationary communications spacecraft, an order of magnitude smaller than a conventional GEO comsat, with a software-defined Ku-band payload of about 7.5 Gbps and electric propulsion. Astranis owns and operates it; the customer is Pacific Dataport, serving Alaskan broadband. It reached its slot and passed an end-to-end test, but a vendor-supplied solar array drive assembly failed, leaving the payload powered only part of each day; Astranis reproduced the failure on the ground and flew a spare, UtilitySat, as a bridge.

@us/ascent/51287.purpose: A 12U CubeSat from AFRL's Space Vehicles Directorate at Kirtland, built on a Blue Canyon bus and flown with the Space Security and Defense Program — AFRL's first CubeSat operated at geostationary altitude. Its job was to find out how commercial off-the-shelf parts and bus electronics actually behave in the GEO radiation and thermal environment, which is the question that decides whether cheap hardware can be trusted there at all. It was released from the LDPE-1 rideshare ring in January 2022 and completed its objectives in October that year. Note the name collision: AFRL's ASCENT green monopropellant is a different thing entirely.

@us/asiastar/26107.purpose: A WorldSpace digital audio broadcasting satellite covering Asia, twin to AfriStar. Built on an Astrium Eurostar-2000+ bus with an Alcatel Space payload of three L-band transponders, it broadcast compressed digital audio, text and images direct to low-cost portable receivers, with on-board baseband processing that let small local stations reach a continent without a hub. WorldSpace collapsed; the satellite was acquired in late 2014 for CMMB as Spectrum 1, largely to hold the orbital slot.

@us/at-t-t-16/44333.purpose: Ordered as DirecTV 16 and renamed before launch after AT&T's acquisition of DirecTV. An Airbus Eurostar-3000 LX Hybrid carrying high-power Ku-band, Ka-band and reverse-band transponders for United States direct-to-home television, with about 16 kW of payload power and a design life of more than fifteen years. It operates from 100.85 degrees West, alongside DirecTV's primary 101 degrees West cluster, and shared its Ariane 5 with Eutelsat 7C.

@us/athena/46275.purpose: An experimental broadband communications satellite operated by PointView Tech, a Facebook subsidiary, and built by Maxar on the small SSL-100 bus. It tested E-band millimetre-wave links, and reportedly a laser ground link, as a precursor to a possible global internet constellation. After reaching orbit it developed a rising spin rate that controllers only partly arrested, and PointView announced in July 2021 that the test mission was paused indefinitely.

@us/aura/28376.purpose: Aura measures ozone, aerosols and key trace gases from the stratosphere down through the troposphere, using OMI, MLS, HIRDLS and TES. It flies in the sun-synchronous A-Train constellation, where several spacecraft cross the same scene minutes apart so their measurements can be combined, and it has carried the long ozone-hole and air-quality record since 2004. NASA reported the spacecraft in good health at its twentieth anniversary but expects falling solar array power to end the mission around mid-2028.

@us/bb-1/56171.purpose: A Tranche 0 Tracking Layer satellite of the Space Development Agency's Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture — the missile-warning half of the constellation. It carries a Leidos wide-field-of-view overhead persistent infrared sensor to detect and track ballistic and hypersonic missiles from low orbit, plus two optical crosslink terminals that hand tracks straight to the Transport Layer instead of waiting for a ground pass. BB is the catalogue name for the SpaceX-built tracking satellites, which use a Starshield bus derived from Starlink. SDA reported first light from these payloads about sixty days after the April 2023 launch.

@us/bb-2/56170.purpose: A Tranche 0 Tracking Layer satellite of the Space Development Agency's Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture — the missile-warning half of the constellation. It carries a Leidos wide-field-of-view overhead persistent infrared sensor to detect and track ballistic and hypersonic missiles from low orbit, plus two optical crosslink terminals that hand tracks straight to the Transport Layer instead of waiting for a ground pass. BB is the catalogue name for the SpaceX-built tracking satellites, which use a Starshield bus derived from Starlink. SDA reported first light from these payloads about sixty days after the April 2023 launch.

@us/bb3/57760.purpose: A Space Development Agency Tranche 0 Tracking Layer satellite, built by SpaceX on a Starshield bus with a Leidos wide-field-of-view overhead persistent infrared sensor. It demonstrates detecting and tracking manoeuvring and hypersonic missile threats from low Earth orbit rather than from geostationary altitude, handing custody data across optical crosslinks to the companion Transport Layer relay satellites. Tranche 0 is an experimental warfighter-immersion tranche, not an operational warning system.

@us/bb4/57757.purpose: One of four SpaceX-built Tranche 0 Tracking Layer satellites for the Space Development Agency, catalogued as T0TR 4. It carries a wide-field-of-view overhead persistent infrared sensor intended to detect and track advanced missile threats, including hypersonic vehicles, from low Earth orbit, plus optical crosslinks that pass tracks to the Transport Layer relay satellites. Tranche 0 is a demonstration tranche proving the proliferated architecture ahead of operational Tranche 1 fielding.

@us/bisonsat/40968.purpose: A 1U cubesat designed, built and operated by students at Salish Kootenai College in Montana, flown under NASA's ELaNa-12 rideshare on the NROL-55 Atlas V. It carries a college-designed visible-light camera and a command and data radio, and its imaging objective is broad-band pictures of aerosols, cloud formation and hydrologic processes over the region. Telemetry was received on several occasions after deployment, making it a working student mission rather than a purely nominal one.

@us/blackcat/67369.purpose: BlackCAT is a 6U CubeSat built by Pennsylvania State University for NASA on a NanoAvionics platform. It carries a coded-aperture soft X-ray telescope covering roughly 0.5–20 keV with an array of event-driven hybrid CMOS detectors, watching a very wide field for high-energy transients: gamma-ray bursts, electromagnetic counterparts to gravitational-wave events, and variable galactic and extragalactic sources. It localises them to about one arcminute and issues rapid alerts so other observatories can follow up.

@us/blackjack-aces-1/56956.purpose: One of four identical spacecraft that became the flight segment of DARPA's Blackjack, the programme arguing that a proliferated low-Earth-orbit constellation on commercial buses could replace capability traditionally flown on a handful of large satellites. Each carries a SEAKR Pit Boss edge-processing node, meant to fuse and act on data on orbit rather than downlinking everything, plus a Storm King radio-frequency payload and four CACI laser terminals, on Blue Canyon Saturn-class buses. Blackjack was cut back sharply from an originally envisaged twenty satellites.

@us/blackjack-aces-2/56955.purpose: One of four identical spacecraft that became the flight segment of DARPA's Blackjack, the programme arguing that a proliferated low-Earth-orbit constellation on commercial buses could replace capability traditionally flown on a handful of large satellites. Each carries a SEAKR Pit Boss edge-processing node for on-orbit data fusion, a Storm King radio-frequency payload and four CACI laser terminals, on Blue Canyon Saturn-class buses. The four launched together on Transporter-8 and then raised orbit to begin demonstrations.

@us/blackjack-aces-3/56950.purpose: One of four identical spacecraft that became the flight segment of DARPA's Blackjack, the programme that argued a proliferated low-Earth-orbit constellation on commercial buses could replace capability traditionally flown on a handful of large satellites. Each carries a SEAKR Pit Boss edge-processing node — the autonomy element, meant to fuse and act on data on orbit rather than downlinking everything — a Storm King radio-frequency payload and four CACI laser communication terminals, on Blue Canyon Saturn-class buses. Blackjack shrank from an originally envisaged twenty satellites to these four, which launched together on Transporter-8 in June 2023.

@us/bluewalker-3/53807.purpose: The prototype that proved AST SpaceMobile's direct-to-handset concept. A roughly 1.5-tonne spacecraft whose 10 m phased array unfolds to about 64 square metres of aperture, it closes a link with an ordinary unmodified mobile phone, no satellite terminal in between, by making the satellite large enough to compensate for the handset being small. It is a test article, not an operational node; the first five commercial BlueBirds repeat its design.

@us/calsphere-1/900.purpose: A passive metal sphere with no power, no instruments and no transmitter, launched by the Naval Research Laboratory in October 1964 alongside the Transit-O 1 navigation satellite. It flew as one of a matched pair — identical in size but very different in mass — so that comparing how the two orbits decayed isolated atmospheric drag and yielded upper-atmosphere density. Sixty years on it is still up there as an inert, precisely known radar target, which is exactly why objects like it are kept in the catalogue.

@us/calsphere-2/902.purpose: The heavier half of a matched pair of passive NRL spheres launched together with the Transit-O 1 navigation satellite in October 1964. Both spheres are geometrically identical; only the mass differs, so the difference in how their orbits evolved is a direct measurement of atmospheric drag and hence of density at that altitude. Thirty years after launch the heavy sphere's orbit had barely moved while the light one had dropped by about fifty kilometres. It carries nothing and transmits nothing.

@us/calsphere-4-a/1520.purpose: A passive calibration sphere built and flown by the Naval Research Laboratory, launched in August 1965 with the Transit-O 5 navigation satellite and a cluster of other small NRL calibration payloads. It has no power, no sensors and no radio. Its value is that a sphere presents the same radar cross-section from every direction and this one's is known exactly, so a tracking radar can be checked against a target whose true signature is not in doubt. It is still in orbit and still inert.

@us/canvas/68635.organization: Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics, University of Colorado Boulder
@us/canvas/68635.purpose: A 4U CubeSat operated by the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder, measuring very low frequency radio waves from lightning and ground transmitters across roughly 0.3 to 40 kHz. It uses a three-axis magnetic search coil on a one-metre boom plus two electric dipole antennas, computing spectral matrices onboard in an FPGA. It was funded by the National Science Foundation and flown through NASA's CubeSat Launch Initiative.

@us/catsat/60246.purpose: A 6U CubeSat built, tested and operated by University of Arizona students and staff with FreeFall Aerospace and Rincon Research. Its primary experiment is an inflatable one-metre spherical antenna intended to give a very small satellite a high-gain link, with cameras to verify inflation; a secondary deployable whip antenna records high-frequency radio signals to probe ionospheric charge distribution. It flew as an ELaNa payload selected through NASA's CubeSat Launch Initiative.

@us/celestis-17-sherpa-fx1/47486.purpose: The spent Sherpa-FX1 free-flying deployer from SpaceX's Transporter-1 rideshare, catalogued together with its hosted Celestis-17 payload. Sherpa-FX is Spaceflight Inc.'s unpropelled port expander: it has a sequencer and one-way telemetry, no attitude control, and releases up to sixteen customer spacecraft before remaining in orbit as an inert structure. Celestis-17 is a passive container of capsules holding cremated human remains, flown as a memorial payload that never separates.

@us/celtee-1/41850.purpose: CubeSat Enhanced Locator Transponder Evaluation Experiment: a 1U cubesat built by M42 Technologies of Seattle for the Air Force Research Laboratory to evaluate an Enhanced Location Transponder for small-satellite tracking and orbit determination. It flew as an NRO-sponsored secondary payload on the Atlas V that carried WorldView-4, and was planned as a short experiment of a few months. The problem it addresses - reliably identifying and tracking individual smallsats deployed in large batches - remains a live space-domain-awareness issue.

@us/checkmate-1/56168.purpose: A Tranche 0 Transport Layer satellite of the Space Development Agency's Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture — the low-orbit mesh network built to move targeting and command data satellite-to-satellite by laser crosslink instead of routing everything through a few ground stations. CHECKMATE is York Space Systems' name for its nine Tranche 0 transport spacecraft, built on York's S-class bus at roughly $15 million each; some carry a Link 16 tactical data link so the constellation can talk directly to fielded terminals. One of the eight flown on Tranche 0 Flight 1 in April 2023. Which individual numbers carry Link 16 is not public.

@us/checkmate-10/57762.purpose: A Tranche 0 Transport Layer satellite of the Space Development Agency's Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture — the low-orbit mesh network built to move targeting and command data satellite-to-satellite by laser crosslink instead of routing everything through a few ground stations. CHECKMATE is York Space Systems' name for its nine Tranche 0 transport spacecraft, built on York's S-class bus at roughly $15 million each; some carry a Link 16 tactical data link so the constellation can talk directly to fielded terminals. It flew five months after the rest, on Tranche 0 Flight 2. There is no CHECKMATE 9 on orbit — it was cancelled, leaving nineteen transport satellites against a planned twenty.

CHECKMATE is York Space Systems' name for its nine Tranche 0 transport spacecraft, built on York's S-class bus at roughly $15 million each; some carry a Link 16 tactical data link so the constellation can talk directly to fielded terminals. One of the eight flown on Tranche 0 Flight 1 in April 2023, now in a slightly lower, more eccentric orbit than its siblings.

@us/checkmate-7/56166.purpose: A Tranche 0 Transport Layer satellite of the Space Development Agency's Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture — the low-orbit mesh network built to move targeting and command data satellite-to-satellite by laser crosslink instead of routing everything through a few ground stations. One of the eight flown on Tranche 0 Flight 1 in April 2023, and the lowest of that group in current elements.

@us/checkmate-8/56162.purpose: A Tranche 0 Transport Layer satellite of the Space Development Agency's Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture — the low-orbit mesh network built to move targeting and command data satellite-to-satellite by laser crosslink instead of routing everything through a few ground stations. @us/cinema/38764.organization: University of California Berkeley Space Sciences Laboratory
@us/cinema/38764.purpose: CINEMA — CubeSat for Ion, Neutral, Electron and Magnetic fields — is a 3U, roughly 4 kg space-weather nanosatellite led by the University of California Berkeley's Space Sciences Laboratory with Imperial College London, Kyung Hee University in Seoul and NASA Ames. It carries STEIN, a suprathermal electron, ion and neutral detector, and MAGIC, a miniature magnetometer built at Imperial, to map energetic neutral atoms and measure magnetic fields in the inner magnetosphere.

@us/coriolis/27640.purpose: Coriolis was a Department of Defense Space Test Program satellite managed by the Naval Research Laboratory. Its primary payload, WindSat, was the first fully polarimetric microwave radiometer flown in space, retrieving ocean surface wind speed and direction — a true vector wind, through cloud — along with sea surface temperature and atmospheric moisture. Its secondary payload, the Solar Mass Ejection Imager, tracked coronal mass ejections across the whole sky to give advance warning of geomagnetic storms. Operations ended on 31 December 2020.

@us/corvus-bc1/42847.purpose: One of the first two Landmapper-BC (Corvus-BC) 6U CubeSats from Astro Digital, carrying a three-band red, green and near-infrared imager at roughly 22 m ground sampling. The design traded resolution for swath, aiming at broad-area agricultural monitoring rather than detail. Gunter's Space Page records both spacecraft of this first pair as failures after deployment, and the Landmapper-BC constellation was later discontinued.

@us/corvus-bc2/42846.purpose: The second of Astro Digital's first Landmapper-BC pair, a 6U CubeSat of about 11 kg carrying a broad-coverage red, green and near-infrared multispectral imager at roughly 22 m per pixel. Gunter's Space Page records it, like its twin, as having failed after deployment. The programme was subsequently discontinued and at least one remaining bus was repurposed, becoming DARPA's Mandrake 1 technology demonstrator.

@us/corvus-bc4/43767.purpose: The fourth Landmapper-BC CubeSat from Astro Digital and one of the few of the line to reach orbit successfully. It carries the same 22 m three-band red, green and near-infrared imager on an 11 kg 6U bus, built for wide-swath repeat coverage of farmland rather than fine detail. The constellation was never completed; remaining buses were reassigned to other programmes.

@us/cosmo/68460.purpose: A University of Colorado Boulder CubeSat flown as a rideshare on a March 2026 Falcon 9 mission, catalogued as a science payload measuring Earth's magnetic field. Public documentation is thin: no operator mission page could be found, and the identification rests on catalogue and launch-manifest records that agree on the institution and on the magnetic-field objective. The form factor, instrument and mission duration should be treated as unestablished.

@us/cs1/49261.purpose: Cesium Satellite 1, the first half of CesiumAstro's Cesium Mission 1, launched as a rideshare with Landsat 9. It is a 6U CubeSat carrying the company's Nightingale-1 Ka-band active phased array plus an inter-satellite link payload, flown as an on-orbit testbed so customers could exercise electronically steered multibeam antenna technology in space. Partly funded through the Defense Innovation Unit; Gunter's Space Page records that both spacecraft suffered power failures after launch.

@us/cs2/49262.purpose: Cesium Satellite 2, the companion to CS1 in CesiumAstro's first mission. The pair were flown together specifically so the inter-satellite link and the Nightingale-1 Ka-band active phased array could be exercised between two spacecraft rather than only to the ground, the electronically steered multibeam architecture now central to proliferated LEO communications. Gunter's Space Page records that both experienced power failures following an otherwise successful launch.

@us/ctc-0/62401.purpose: An 8U CubeSat built by EnduroSat for Space Telecommunication Inc. as a direct-to-device connectivity demonstrator, tested outside the United States. It carries two full-duplex transceivers with directional panel antennas and is designed to communicate with unmodified mobile handsets on the ground as well as with fixed ground stations — the same problem the large direct-to-cell constellations are attacking, tried at cubesat scale. It reached orbit on the Bandwagon-2 rideshare in December 2024.

@us/cupid/49264.purpose: The Cusp Plasma Imaging Detector, a 6U CubeSat led by Boston University with Drexel University, NASA Goddard and Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory. It carries the first wide-field soft X-ray imager flown in orbit, mapping the X-rays emitted when solar-wind ions exchange charge with neutral atoms at the edge of the magnetosphere. The goal is to distinguish between competing models of how dayside magnetopause reconnection is distributed in space and time.

@us/cygnus-ng-24/68689.purpose: Northrop Grumman's Cygnus XL cargo freighter flying NASA Commercial Resupply Services mission NG-24, also designated Cygnus CRS-24, launched on a Falcon 9 from Cape Canaveral rather than Antares. Cygnus is uncrewed but is an International Space Station logistics vehicle: it is berthed by the station arm, delivers pressurised cargo and science, then departs, can deploy CubeSats from an external dispenser, and is destroyed on reentry with station waste.

@us/db-charms-nd/68455.purpose: Dream Big 1, the first of six 0.5U satellites built by NearSpace Launch and flown together on SpaceX Transporter-16 as a low-cost student flight series; the catalogue name records the hosted experiment, CHARMS. Each Dream Big unit carries a different university payload, and the series is operated in association with Western Michigan University. Satellites this small have no propulsion and short orbital lives, and are used to give student teams a real flight opportunity rather than to deliver an operational capability.

@us/db-globe-mission-earth-u/68459.organization: NearSpace Launch / GLOBE Mission EARTH (University of Toledo)
@us/db-globe-mission-earth-u/68459.purpose: This is Dream Big 6, one of six half-unit ThinSat-class picosatellites of roughly 500 g built by NearSpace Launch of Upland, Indiana, and flown together as student flight-education payloads. Its full catalogue name is DB-GLOBE Mission Earth-UT: it belongs to GLOBE Mission EARTH, the multi-institution collaborative led from the University of Toledo that supports NASA's GLOBE environmental-science education programme. Each Dream Big unit carries a student-built experiment rather than an operational sensor.

@us/db-precisionflightworksp/68466.purpose: One of six small student-built spacecraft in the Dream Big constellation, manufactured with NearSpace Launch of Upland, Indiana and launched together on a single March 2026 rideshare. Each is a roughly half-unit CubeSat-class satellite assigned to a university team, giving students hands-on design, build and operations experience with a simple technology or education payload. Catalogue records disagree over which team this member belongs to.

@us/db-skyforge-core-tu/68445.purpose: One of six 0.5U ThinSat-class picosatellites in the Dream Big constellation, built by NearSpace Launch of Upland, Indiana and flown as a low-cost technology and student-education series. Each unit carries a different university-sponsored payload identified only by an abbreviation in its catalogue name; the SkyForge CORE experiment behind this one is not described in any public source located. The class has no propulsion.

@us/db-wali-wmu/68443.purpose: Dream Big 4, a 0.5U CubeSat built by a Western Michigan University student team and integrated by NearSpace Launch. It is one of six near-identical student spacecraft flown together as the Dream Big constellation on the March 2026 Transporter rideshare, each designed and built by a different university. The programme is an education and flight-experience mission rather than an operational one, with NearSpace Launch supplying the bus, integration and communications.

@us/deimos/60526.purpose: A 1.5U cubesat flown by Aethero, a US space-computing startup, and manufactured by EnduroSat. It hosts a pair of electro-optical sensors and Aethero's own edge-computing module built around an Nvidia Jetson Orin NX processor, enclosed in Cosmic Shielding's nanocomposite radiation shielding so a commercial-grade GPU can survive the environment. The mission tests over-the-air software updates and machine-learning workloads run on board, the enabling step for processing imagery in orbit instead of downlinking everything.

@us/demo8-tenzing/48951.purpose: Astro Digital's Demo-8, catalogued as Tanker-001 Tenzing, is a roughly 35 kg Corvus-class spacecraft flown as an orbital test bed for refuelling and manoeuvring hardware. It carries Orbit Fab's RAFTI rapidly attachable fluid transfer interface with an auxiliary propellant tank and docking adapter, a Benchmark hydrogen-peroxide thruster, a tiled ionic-liquid electrospray electric thruster, and stereo cameras for non-Earth imaging — the building blocks for later rendezvous, proximity operations and disposal manoeuvres.

@us/directv-11/32729.purpose: The second of three Boeing BSS-702 spacecraft DirecTV ordered in 2004 to expand high-definition broadcasting. It carries a large Ka-band payload - national and spot-beam transponders - that let DirecTV deliver local HD channels to about ninety percent of its subscribers across the contiguous United States, Hawaii and Alaska. Renamed AT&T T-11 after AT&T acquired DirecTV. It was launched by a Sea Launch Zenit-3SL from the Pacific.

@us/directv-12/36131.purpose: Third of the Boeing BSS-702 trio DirecTV ordered in 2004, procured as the ground spare for DirecTV 10 and 11 and later launched in its own right on a Proton-M/Briz-M. It carries the same Ka-band national and spot-beam payload used for high-definition national and local television across the contiguous United States, Hawaii and Alaska. Renamed AT&T T-12 after AT&T acquired DirecTV.

@us/directv-14/40333.purpose: A 20-kilowatt Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300 built to expand DirecTV's high-definition capacity. It carries 76 Ka-band spot-beam transponders for local HD channels plus 18 national reverse-band transponders, and was stationed at 99 degrees West. Reverse-band operation means broadcasting on frequencies normally allocated to uplinks, which gave DirecTV additional usable spectrum. It flew on an Ariane 5 alongside India's GSAT-16.

@us/directv-15/40663.purpose: An Airbus (then EADS Astrium) Eurostar-3000 ordered in 2011 to provide back-up capacity and fleet expansion for DirecTV. Its payload combines 30 high-power Ku-band transponders, 24 Ka-band transponders and 18 reverse-band transponders, and the satellite was designed to work from any of five orbital slots between 99 and 119 degrees West, covering the contiguous United States, Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico. It shared its Ariane 5 with Sky Mexico 1.

@us/directv-5-tempo-1/27426.purpose: Built by Space Systems/Loral as Tempo 1 for TCI's Tempo Satellite venture with 32 high-power Ku-band transponders, switchable to 16 at double power. Its intended 110 degrees West DBS licence was lost to MCI at FCC auction before launch, so the satellite sat on the ground until DirecTV acquired the Tempo assets with PrimeStar in 1999 and renamed it DirecTV 5. It finally flew on a Proton-K in 2002.

@us/directv-8/28659.purpose: A Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300 providing selectable medium- and high-power Ku-band broadcast capacity to the United States on up to 32 transponders, together with a Ka-band payload that uses the full 1,000 MHz of Ka bandwidth available to DirecTV for backhaul and for the roll-out of local digital and high-definition services. The spacecraft was completed on the partly built bus of the cancelled L-Star 1 satellite. Renamed AT&T T-8.

@us/directv-9s/29494.purpose: A Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300 spot-beam satellite procured as the back-up for DirecTV 4S and 7S. In its primary configuration it provides up to 54 transponders of national and local digital video broadcast into 27 beams, or 44 transponders into 30 beams in an alternate mode, and it was designed to work from either 101 or 119 degrees West. Renamed AT&T T-9S.

@us/disksat-a/67222.purpose: One of four DiskSats, a new form factor from The Aerospace Corporation, funded by NASA and flown for the Space Test Program: a composite disc a metre across and 2.5 cm thick with the internal volume of a 20U CubeSat on under 3 kg of structure. Discs stack like plates in a dispenser, so a rideshare can carry many, and the large area supplies power without deployable solar arrays. It is aimed at very low orbit, flying edge-on to cut drag with electric propulsion holding altitude. This unit is the last piece in the COSPAR sequence; the letters do not run in launch order.

@us/disksat-b/67220.purpose: One of four DiskSats, a new form factor from The Aerospace Corporation, funded by NASA and flown for the Space Test Program: a composite disc a metre across and 2.5 cm thick with the internal volume of a 20U CubeSat on under 3 kg of structure. Discs stack like plates in a dispenser, so a rideshare can carry many, and the large area supplies power without deployable solar arrays. It is aimed at very low orbit, flying edge-on to cut drag with electric propulsion holding altitude. This unit is 2025-305B; the four were ejected one at a time, a few minutes apart.

@us/disksat-c/67219.purpose: One of four DiskSats, a new form factor from The Aerospace Corporation, funded by NASA and flown for the Space Test Program: a composite disc a metre across and 2.5 cm thick with the internal volume of a 20U CubeSat on under 3 kg of structure. Discs stack like plates in a dispenser, so a rideshare can carry many, and the large area supplies power without deployable solar arrays. It is aimed at very low orbit, flying edge-on to cut drag with electric propulsion holding altitude. This unit is the first piece in the COSPAR sequence, and so the first of the four ejected.

@us/disksat-d/67221.purpose: One of four DiskSats, a new form factor from The Aerospace Corporation, funded by NASA and flown for the Space Test Program: a composite disc a metre across and 2.5 cm thick with the internal volume of a 20U CubeSat on under 3 kg of structure. Discs stack like plates in a dispenser, so a rideshare can carry many, and the large area supplies power without deployable solar arrays. It is aimed at very low orbit, flying edge-on to cut drag with electric propulsion holding altitude. This unit is 2025-305C; the letters do not run in COSPAR order.

@us/dragon-freedom-3/67796.purpose: The SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule Freedom flying NASA's Crew-12 mission, the twelfth operational Commercial Crew rotation and the twentieth crewed Dragon flight. It carried NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA's Sophie Adenot and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev to the International Space Station, docking at the Harmony zenith port, where it stays as the crew's lifeboat until the planned return in September 2026.

@us/dragracer-2-augury/46955.purpose: The control half of TriSept's Dragracer experiment: two identical 6U CubeSats on a Millennium Space bus, one fitted with Tethers Unlimited's Terminator Tape electrodynamic drag tether and one, Augury, deliberately left bare. Alchemy deployed its tether and reentered within about eight months; Augury has been left to decay naturally, and the divergence between the two decay curves is the measurement. Its slow decay is the intended result, not a malfunction.

@us/droid-002/63223.purpose: The second Droid spacecraft from Turion Space, a microsatellite demonstrator for commercial space domain awareness and, in later generations, debris removal and satellite servicing. Built on a NanoAvionics MP42 bus with a green monopropellant thruster, the Droid line is designed to manoeuvre near other resident space objects and image them at close range, producing custody and characterisation data that ground radars and telescopes cannot resolve. Droid.001 carried HEO Robotics' HOLMES imager.

@us/dsx/44344.purpose: The Demonstration and Science Experiments spacecraft, an AFRL free-flyer deliberately parked in medium Earth orbit, inside the slot region between the electron belts where most spacecraft never linger. Its Wave Particle Interaction Experiment transmitted high-power VLF through an 80-metre dipole to test whether man-made waves can scatter energetic electrons into the atmosphere and so remediate the belts; a companion suite mapped the MEO particle environment for future DoD orbit selection, and a third measured radiation and plasma damage to thin-film photovoltaics. Passivated on 31 May 2021.

@us/duplex/66906.purpose: The Dual Propulsion Experiment, a 6U CubeSat from CU Aerospace flying two micropropulsion systems: a Fiber-fed Pulsed Plasma Thruster and a Monofilament Vaporization Propulsion thruster. Both use spooled solid polymer propellant - PTFE and Delrin - which is non-toxic, non-corrosive and unpressurised, avoiding the handling and range-safety burden of conventional smallsat propulsion. Funded under NASA's 2019 Tipping Point programme and released from the International Space Station after arriving on a Cygnus resupply flight.

@us/earthcare/59908.purpose: EarthCARE — the Earth Cloud, Aerosol and Radiation Explorer — is a joint ESA and JAXA satellite carrying a cloud profiling radar, an atmospheric lidar, a multispectral imager and a broadband radiometer. Flying all four together is the design point: it measures the vertical structure of cloud and aerosol and the radiation actually leaving the top of the atmosphere in the same scene, which is what constrains how clouds and aerosols regulate Earth's energy balance. Launched May 2024 and operational.

@us/echostar-10/28935.purpose: A Lockheed Martin A2100AXS direct-broadcast satellite for DISH Network carrying 42 Ku-band spot-beam transponders. It served the 110 degrees West DBS slot, distributing national and local television to small consumer dishes across the United States. EchoStar 18, a much larger multi-spot SSL-1300 with 61 Ku transponders, was later launched to the same position to replace it.

@us/echostar-11/33207.purpose: A Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300 direct-broadcast satellite with 32 Ku-band transponders, ordered in 2004 to support DISH Network programming and to serve as back-up capacity for the rest of the fleet. At about 5,500 kg it was among the heavier commercial DBS spacecraft of its generation. It was launched from the Sea Launch platform in the equatorial Pacific by a Zenit-3SL, a route several EchoStar satellites took.

@us/echostar-14/36499.purpose: A Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300 direct-broadcast satellite ordered in 2007 to expand services for DISH Network's more than thirteen million direct-to-home subscribers. Its Ku-band payload is unusually large for a DBS spacecraft at 103 transponders, and launch mass was about 6,400 kg. It was placed in orbit by a Proton-M/Briz-M from Baikonur.

@us/echostar-15/36792.purpose: A Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300 direct-broadcast satellite ordered in 2008, the eighth SS/L-built spacecraft in the EchoStar fleet, carrying 32 Ku-band transponders to expand DISH Network's programming capacity. It is essentially a repeat of EchoStar 11 on the same bus, and was launched by a Proton-M/Briz-M from Baikonur.

@us/echostar-16/39008.purpose: An all-Ku-band Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300 with 32 high-power transponders, serving DISH Network's direct-to-home business from 61.5 degrees West, the eastern of DISH's direct-broadcast positions. At about 6,260 kg it is one of the heavier satellites in the EchoStar fleet, and it was launched by a Proton-M/Briz-M.

@us/echostar-17/38551.purpose: Also called Jupiter 1: a high-throughput Ka-band broadband satellite, not a television spacecraft. Built by Space Systems/Loral on the SSL-1300 bus with a multi-spot-beam bent-pipe Ka architecture delivering more than 100 Gbps over North America, it is the space segment behind HughesNet consumer satellite internet. It was ordered by Hughes as Jupiter 1 in 2009 and renamed EchoStar 17 after EchoStar acquired Hughes Network Systems in 2011.

@us/echostar-18/41592.purpose: A high-power multi-spot-beam Ku-band direct-broadcast satellite on the Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300 bus, carrying 61 Ku transponders. It was launched to 110 degrees West to replace EchoStar 10 at that DBS slot, raising the transponder count available there for DISH Network's national and local television services from 42 to 61. Launch mass was about 6,300 kg.

@us/echostar-19/41893.purpose: Also called Jupiter 2: a large multi-spot-beam Ka-band high-throughput satellite built by Space Systems/Loral on the SSL-1300 bus, carrying about fifty percent more capacity than Jupiter 1 and supporting HughesNet Gen4 consumer broadband in North America. At roughly 6,600 kg with four SPT-100 plasma thrusters for station keeping, it was launched by an Atlas V 431. Like EchoStar 17 it is a broadband satellite, not a DISH television spacecraft.

@us/echostar-21/42749.purpose: Built by Space Systems/Loral as TerreStar 2 on the SSL-1300S bus, an S-band mobile satellite services spacecraft with a large unfurlable reflector generating many spot beams. It was completed in 2009 and put into storage; DISH acquired the TerreStar assets in 2012 and finally launched it in 2017 as EchoStar 21. It now supports EchoStar Mobile's pan-European S-band mobile satellite and LoRa-based satellite IoT network rather than any United States service.

@us/echostar-23/42070.purpose: A Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300 built on the long-stored bus of the cancelled CMBStar 1 (EchoStar 13) satellite. Unusually it is tri-band, carrying 32 Ku-band transponders plus Ka-band and S-band payloads, and it was designed so that it can provide service from any of eight different orbital slots - an insurance policy for orbital-slot and licence obligations rather than a satellite tied to one position. It was launched on a Falcon 9 from Kennedy Space Center.

@us/echostar-25/68126.purpose: The newest DISH Network direct-broadcast satellite, ordered from Maxar in April 2023 and built on the SSL-1300 bus. It carries a high-power Ku-band broadcast-satellite-service payload with multiple spot beams, using frequency reuse across targeted coverage regions to raise the number of television channels that can be delivered to small consumer dishes across North America. About 6,800 kg at launch, flown by a Falcon 9.

@us/edda-1-300f/69018.organization: Planet Labs (for the Swedish Armed Forces)
@us/edda-1-300f/69018.purpose: A Planet Labs Pelican spacecraft, serial 300f, operating under the name Edda 1 as the first satellite of a services agreement with the Swedish Armed Forces. Pelican is Planet's successor to SkySat: an approximately 120-150 kg smallsat with Hall-effect thrusters carrying a five-band visible to near-infrared pushbroom imager capable of ground sampling down to about 0.3 m. The Swedish programme envisages up to ten satellites and a national space operations centre.

@us/epic-athena/64871.purpose: Athena EPIC — Economical Payload Integration Cost — is a roughly 50 kg sensorcraft assembled from six of NovaWurks' aggregated HISat satlets, a cellular architecture in which identical building blocks supply all spacecraft functions. Its payload, delivered by NASA Langley, is a simplified single-channel derivative of the CERES radiometer flown on Terra, Aqua, Suomi NPP and NOAA-20, measuring the solar energy Earth reflects and emits. It is a joint NASA, NOAA and Space Force demonstration.

@us/ews-g2/36411.purpose: Formerly GOES-15, the last of the three Boeing BSS-601 GOES N-series weather satellites. NOAA retired it from the GOES-West position in 2018 and kept it as a back-up until 2020; ownership transferred to the U.S. Space Force in September 2023 as the second Electro-optical Infrared Weather System - Geostationary spacecraft. It was then drifted to about 62 degrees East, giving the Space Force its own geostationary imagery and sounding over the Indian Ocean region.

@us/ews-g3/35491.purpose: This object is GOES-14, the middle spacecraft of NOAA's three Boeing BSS-601 GOES N-series weather satellites, carrying the five-channel imager, the sounder and a solar X-ray imager. It spent most of its life as NOAA's on-orbit spare, briefly standing in as GOES-East in 2012 when GOES-13 failed. The catalogue name EWS-G3 marks its transfer to the U.S. Space Force, following GOES-13 as EWS-G1 and GOES-15 as EWS-G2.

@us/excite/43819.purpose: eXCITe, also designated Payload Test Bed 1, is a DARPA technology demonstrator built by NovaWurks from fourteen aggregated HiSat 'satlets' - small identical modules that pool power, data handling and thermal control to assemble a spacecraft bus from parts. It tested whether such an aggregate could survive launch, hold thermal control, talk to the ground and support payloads. A planned amateur radio payload was removed pre-launch, and the SeeMe satellite it carried apparently never separated.

@us/eyesat-a/22825.purpose: Eyesat 1 is a 12 kg microsatellite built by Interferometrics Inc. of Chantilly, Virginia on the AMSAT-NA Microsat bus, flown as a store-and-forward communications experiment for monitoring mobile industrial equipment; it also carried NOAA traffic to the South Pole. A second payload, an FM repeater contributed by the amateur group AMRAD, gives it the name AMRAD-OSCAR 27, and it is switched on for part of each sunlit pass to protect the battery. A planned six-satellite constellation never followed.

@us/ezie-a/63247.organization: NASA / Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory
@us/ezie-a/63247.purpose: EZIE-A is one of three identical NASA SmallSats, built and led by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, flying in a string formation to map the auroral electrojets — the intense currents that run about 100 kilometres above the polar regions and close the electrical circuit between the magnetosphere and the ionosphere. They sense the electrojet's magnetic field remotely through Zeeman splitting, at an altitude too high for aircraft and too low for a satellite to fly through. Launched March 2025 and operating.

@us/ezie-b/63250.organization: NASA / Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory
@us/ezie-b/63250.purpose: EZIE-B is one of three identical NASA SmallSats, built and led by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, flying in a string formation to map the auroral electrojets — the intense currents that run about 100 kilometres above the polar regions and close the electrical circuit between the magnetosphere and the ionosphere. They sense the electrojet's magnetic field remotely through Zeeman splitting, at an altitude too high for aircraft and too low for a satellite to fly through. Launched March 2025 and operating.

@us/ezie-c/63249.organization: NASA / Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory
@us/ezie-c/63249.purpose: EZIE-C is one of three identical NASA SmallSats, built and led by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, flying in a string formation to map the auroral electrojets — the intense currents that run about 100 kilometres above the polar regions and close the electrical circuit between the magnetosphere and the ionosphere. They sense the electrojet's magnetic field remotely through Zeeman splitting, at an altitude too high for aircraft and too low for a satellite to fly through. Launched March 2025 and operating.

@us/falconsat-10/58291.purpose: A cadet-built microsatellite from the US Air Force Academy's Space Systems Research Center, sponsored by the Air Force Research Laboratory. Also designated FalconSAT-X, it hosts a set of technology experiments described publicly only in general terms — propulsion and communications among them — which is normal for the programme: the teaching value is that cadets carry a payload from design through integration to on-orbit operation from the Academy's own ground station. It reached a sun-synchronous orbit on the Transporter-9 rideshare in November 2023.

@us/falconsat-6/43815.purpose: A cadet-built microsatellite from the US Air Force Academy's Space Systems Research Center, sponsored by AFRL — the FalconSAT programme exists so undergraduates design, build and operate a real spacecraft carrying real DoD experiments. FalconSat-6's principal payload was a reflight of the modified commercial Hall-effect thruster from FalconSat-5, exercising multiple thrust modes to show efficient small-satellite orbital manoeuvre; alongside it flew a contamination monitor, the Cerberus space-situational-awareness experiment, advanced solar array and flexible-circuit tests, and an ionospheric propagation experiment that measured how the thruster's own plume perturbs the local ionosphere.

@us/fastsat-hsv01-usa-220/37225.purpose: FASTSAT-HSV01 was a NASA Marshall Space Flight Center microsatellite flown on the Space Test Program's STP-S26 mission to show a low-cost bus could carry several unrelated payloads at once. Three of its six payloads were space-environment instruments: MINI-ME, a low-energy neutral atom imager; TTI, a thermosphere temperature imager tied to spacecraft drag; and PISA, which measured thermal electron density in the ionosphere. It also ejected the NanoSail-D solar sail. Last contact was in May 2013.

@us/ffly-1/65320.purpose: A Firefly hyperspectral imaging satellite operated by Pixxel, an Earth-observation company headquartered in Bengaluru. The roughly 60 kg spacecraft carries an imager of more than 150 bands across 450-900 nm at about 5 m ground resolution over a 40 km swath, sold commercially for agriculture, mining and environmental monitoring. Tracking catalogues label this object FFLY-1; the established references identify the same designator as Firefly 4.

@us/ffly-2/65322.purpose: One of three Pixxel Firefly hyperspectral imaging satellites deployed on the August 2025 rideshare. Each roughly 60 kg spacecraft carries a visible to near-infrared hyperspectral imager of more than 150 bands at about 5 m ground resolution across a 40 km swath, feeding Pixxel's commercial constellation for agriculture, mineral prospecting and environmental monitoring. Which specific Firefly unit this catalogue entry corresponds to is not settled between sources.

@us/ffly-3/65319.purpose: One of Pixxel's Firefly hyperspectral imaging satellites, from the second batch of three launched in August 2025. Each Firefly is a roughly 60 kg spacecraft carrying an imager with more than 150 contiguous bands between about 450 and 900 nm, five-metre ground sampling and a 40 km swath. Hyperspectral data of this kind separates materials by their spectral signature rather than their shape, supporting agriculture, methane and mineral detection and environmental monitoring.

@us/firesat0/63256.organization: Muon Space for the Earth Fire Alliance
@us/firesat0/63256.purpose: FireSat 0 is the protoflight spacecraft for the Earth Fire Alliance's FireSat constellation, designed, built and operated by Muon Space on its own small-satellite platform. It carries a purpose-built six-channel multispectral infrared instrument intended to detect and track wildfires, including small early-stage fires, far more often than existing operational weather satellites revisit. Muon established contact and confirmed the satellite healthy after deployment; the first three operational FireSat spacecraft followed in 2026.

@us/firesat1/69886.organization: Muon Space for the Earth Fire Alliance
@us/firesat1/69886.purpose: The first of three operational wildfire satellites designed, built and operated by Muon Space for the nonprofit Earth Fire Alliance, following a protoflight demonstrator that flew a year earlier. It carries a six-channel multispectral infrared imager sized to spot fires as small as about five metres across a wide swath, feeding near real-time hotspot detection, fire perimeter and fire progression products to firefighting agencies rather than to a general imagery market.

@us/firesat2/69873.purpose: The second of the first three operational FireSat satellites, built by Muon Space and operated for the non-profit Earth Fire Alliance. Each carries a six-channel multispectral infrared payload able to resolve fires roughly five metres across and to see through smoke and thin cloud. The three together give at least twice-daily revisit over every fire-prone region, the first increment of a constellation intended to grow past fifty satellites by 2030.

@us/firesat3/69890.purpose: One of the first three operational satellites of the Earth Fire Alliance's FireSat constellation, designed, built and operated by Muon Space on its Halo and Condor-M platform. Each roughly 130 kg spacecraft carries a six-channel multispectral infrared instrument built to detect and track wildfires, including small early-stage fires, and to revisit them often enough to support response decisions. They follow the FireSat 0 protoflight demonstrator flown in 2025.

@us/fltsatcom-8-usa-46/20253.purpose: FLTSATCOM 8 is the last of the US Navy's first-generation Fleet Satellite Communications spacecraft, built by TRW and launched to geostationary orbit in 1989 as one of three improved Block 2 satellites. Each carried 23 UHF and SHF channels: ten for Navy worldwide traffic among ships, aircraft and submarines, twelve for the Air Force Satellite Communications System, and one narrow channel reserved for the National Command Authority. Block 2 also flew an experimental EHF package as a Milstar terminal testbed. It is long past its five-year design life.

@us/forte/24920.organization: US Department of Energy (Los Alamos and Sandia National Laboratories)
@us/forte/24920.purpose: FORTE — Fast On-orbit Recording of Transient Events — was a Department of Energy satellite built jointly by Los Alamos and Sandia national laboratories as a testbed for detecting clandestine nuclear tests from orbit. It carried three broadband radio receivers spanning 30 to 300 MHz on a 35-foot crossed antenna, an optical lightning imager and photodetector, and an onboard event classifier. Much of its lasting value was in lightning physics and in measuring how the ionosphere disperses and distorts radio signals travelling up to a satellite.

@us/fox-1/40967.purpose: Fox-1A, designated AMSAT-OSCAR 85: the first of AMSAT's Fox-1 series of 1U cubesats, launched under NASA's ELaNa XII programme on the NROL-55 Atlas V. It carried a mode U/V FM repeater usable with a handheld radio and a small yagi, with telemetry sent as data under voice, plus a Vanderbilt low-energy proton radiation experiment and a Penn State-Erie gyroscope experiment. Its 64-degree orbit put apogee over the northern hemisphere. AMSAT-UK now lists it among non-operational satellites.

@us/galaxy-19/33376.purpose: An Intelsat hybrid C- and Ku-band satellite on the Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300 bus, ordered as Intelsat Americas 9 and renamed Galaxy 19 in 2007. It carries 52 operating transponders selectable among 62 discrete frequencies, giving 1,944 MHz of downlink, with fixed C- and Ku-band antennas plus a steerable Ku spot beam that can be pointed anywhere visible from the slot. It replaced Galaxy 25 over North America.

@us/galaxy-31/54243.purpose: One of seven replacement satellites Intelsat ordered to clear the lower 300 MHz of United States C-band spectrum for 5G. Built by Maxar on the SSL-1300 bus, it is a C-band-only spacecraft whose job is to carry Intelsat's existing television distribution customers in the narrower slice of C-band left after the FCC auction. Also designated Galaxy 23R. Clearing the band by December 2023 was worth 4.87 billion dollars in accelerated relocation payments to Intelsat.

@us/galaxy-34/54027.purpose: A C-band-only Intelsat satellite built by Northrop Grumman on the GEOStar-3 bus - one of the two of the seven C-band clearing spacecraft that did not come from Maxar. Like its siblings it exists to move Intelsat's American television distribution customers into the compressed C-band plan created when the FCC auctioned 300 MHz of the band for 5G. Also designated Galaxy 12R. It launched paired with Galaxy 33 on a Falcon 9.

@us/galaxy-35/54741.purpose: A Maxar-built C-band-only satellite on the SSL-1300 bus, part of the fleet Intelsat procured to vacate the lower 300 MHz of United States C-band for 5G cellular use. Also designated Galaxy 3CR, it replaces earlier Galaxy capacity in the compressed band plan. It shared its Ariane 5 with Galaxy 36 and with EUMETSAT's first Meteosat Third Generation imager, MTG-I1.

@us/galaxy-36/54742.purpose: A Maxar-built C-band-only satellite on the SSL-1300 bus, the fourth of the four Maxar spacecraft in Intelsat's C-band clearing programme. Also designated Galaxy 28R, it takes over television distribution traffic in the narrower C-band plan that followed the FCC's auction of 300 MHz for 5G. It launched alongside Galaxy 35 and EUMETSAT's MTG-I1 on an Ariane 5.

@us/gems2-amethyst/68505.purpose: GEMS2-Amethyst is a 6U CubeSat operated by Weather Stream, the Boulder, Colorado firm formed around Orbital Micro Systems, and is the next stage of its Global Environmental Monitoring System constellation. It carries a microwave radiometer for atmospheric sounding and imagery — the sensor class that returns temperature and humidity profiles through cloud. Its predecessor GEMS1, deployed from the International Space Station in 2019, was the first commercial microwave radiometer placed in orbit.

@us/gen1a-1/69004.purpose: Lynk Tower Gen1A-1, the first of Lynk Global's Gen1A satellites and also catalogued as Lynk Tower 07. Lynk operates spacecraft that behave like orbiting cell towers, connecting directly to unmodified standard mobile handsets so that messaging, low-rate data and emergency traffic can work where there is no terrestrial coverage. It launched alongside its sibling Gen1A-2 on a sun-synchronous rideshare from Vandenberg.

@us/gen1a-2/69005.purpose: Lynk Tower 8, the second Gen1A satellite from Lynk Global. It works as a cell tower in orbit, connecting directly to ordinary unmodified handsets on standard mobile bands, so the service is narrowband by nature: messaging, alerting and IoT rather than broadband. The Gen1A units are the step from Lynk's earlier experimental payloads toward an operational direct-to-device constellation.

@us/genmat-1/58276.purpose: A 6U CubeSat flown for Quantum Generative Materials and built by Exobotics, carrying a hyperspectral imager covering roughly 450 to 900 nm. It is a prototype for a planned constellation aimed at mineral prospecting and categorising geological resources, with orbital spectra correlated against ground-truth field observations on private land in Nevada and elsewhere. The mission is commercial minerals assay rather than a general-purpose Earth observation service.

@us/ghgsat-c1/46278.purpose: A GHGSat methane-monitoring microsatellite. GHGSat Inc. is Canadian, headquartered in Montreal, and its wide-angle Fabry-Perot shortwave-infrared spectrometer images individual industrial sites rather than mapping whole regions, resolving a plume closely enough to attribute it to the equipment that produced it and detecting releases above roughly 100 kg per hour. C1, named Iris, is the first of the operational C-series that followed the Claire demonstrator, built like the rest on SFL's 15 kg NEMO bus and launched on Vega's small-spacecraft rideshare proof-of-concept flight.

@us/ghgsat-c12/64529.purpose: A GHGSat methane-monitoring microsatellite. GHGSat Inc. is Canadian, headquartered in Montreal, and its wide-angle Fabry-Perot shortwave-infrared spectrometer images individual industrial sites rather than mapping whole regions, resolving a plume closely enough to attribute it to the equipment that produced it and detecting releases above roughly 100 kg per hour. @us/ghost-3/56958.purpose: The third Global Hyperspectral Observation Satellite of Orbital Sidekick's commercial constellation, launched on the Transporter-8 rideshare. It is an 85 kg spacecraft on an Astro Digital Corvus-XL bus carrying a hyperspectral imager with more than 400 bands from 400 to 2500 nm - visible through shortwave infrared - at roughly 8 m ground sampling, downlinked over Ka-band. The company's principal market is pipeline and energy-infrastructure monitoring, where hydrocarbon leaks appear as spectral rather than visual features.

@us/ghost-4/59133.purpose: GHOSt 4 is one of six Global Hyperspectral Observation Satellites operated by Orbital Sidekick, an 85 kg ESPA-class spacecraft built on Astro Digital's Corvus-XL bus with a Ka-band downlink. Its hyperspectral imager collects more than 400 bands from 400 to 2500 nanometres at roughly 8 metre ground sampling. The product is spectral signatures rather than pictures: gas leaks, pipeline and infrastructure anomalies, and material identification feeding the company's monitoring service.

@us/ghost-5/59130.purpose: The fifth Global Hyperspectral Observation Satellite in Orbital Sidekick's GHOSt constellation, an ESPA-class spacecraft built by Astro Digital on the Corvus-XL bus. Its hyperspectral imager covers roughly 400 to 2500 nanometres in more than 400 bands at about eight metres ground sample distance, downlinked over Ka-band, and is sold commercially for monitoring pipelines and other infrastructure for leaks, encroachment and change.

@us/gitai-sc1/62388.purpose: A 16U CubeSat designed and built in-house by GITAI USA of Torrance, California to show that the space-robotics company can also build and fly its own spacecraft. It deployed a tethered target and observed it with cameras, LiDAR and a laser rangefinder while exercising reaction-wheel attitude control, propulsion and machine-vision processing. GITAI declared full success against all three mission criteria in January 2025, qualifying the bus for later on-orbit servicing work.

@us/glast/33053.purpose: Launched in 2008 as GLAST and renamed the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope shortly afterwards, this NASA observatory surveys the whole sky in gamma rays from about 8 keV to over 300 GeV with the Large Area Telescope and the Gamma-ray Burst Monitor. It has catalogued more than 300 gamma-ray pulsars and revealed the Fermi Bubbles, and it contributes rapid gamma-ray follow-up to gravitational wave and neutrino alerts. NASA reports the spacecraft and instruments in good health and still monitoring the sky.

@us/gnomes-1/46266.purpose: PlanetiQ's first GNSS radio occultation satellite. Radio occultation watches a GPS, Galileo, GLONASS or BeiDou signal set behind the Earth's limb: the ray bends as it crosses air of changing density, and inverting that bending yields a profile of temperature, pressure and water vapour against height. The measurement is traceable to an atomic clock and needs no bias correction, which makes it unusually valuable per observation to numerical weather prediction. eoPortal records GNOMES-1 as having suffered an operational failure.

@us/gnomes-3/52158.purpose: The third PlanetiQ radio occultation microsatellite, carrying the company's Pyxis receiver on a Blue Canyon X-SAT class bus in a sun-synchronous orbit near 645 km. Each occultation returns a vertical profile of temperature, pressure and humidity through the depth of the atmosphere. For METOC that matters most over ocean, where there are no radiosondes and where model error in the thermodynamic structure translates directly into bad forecasts of tropical cyclone intensity and of ducting conditions.

@us/gnomes-4/58462.purpose: The fourth of PlanetiQ's GNOMES radio occultation satellites, and the first launched after the company moved to a routine operational cadence. Its Pyxis receiver tracks occultations from all four global navigation constellations, roughly tripling the collection rate of earlier commercial RO sensors. Radio occultation profiles are among the highest-impact inputs to global models precisely because they are self-calibrating: they anchor the model's temperature field without needing a satellite-to-satellite intercalibration chain.

@us/gnomes-5/60574.purpose: The fifth PlanetiQ GNOMES satellite, and the one whose data underpins the company's NOAA supply contract: PlanetiQ delivers radio occultation profiles to NOAA's commercial weather data programme at a rate of about 2,200 soundings a day. Beyond temperature and humidity profiles, the dual-polarisation antenna allows heavy precipitation to be sensed along the occulting ray and surface reflections to be used for ocean wind, soil moisture and sea ice.

@us/gps/24876.purpose: A GPS satellite. NAVSTAR is the Global Positioning System's own programme designation, which is why the best-known constellation in orbit is catalogued under a name most people never see. The U.S. Space Force's 2nd Space Operations Squadron flies it as at least 24 slots in six equally spaced orbital planes at about 20,200 km, each satellite circling the Earth twice a day, with several extra spacecraft aloft so that coverage survives maintenance and decommissioning. For a maritime operator the point to hold onto is that this is a one-way broadcast of very weak signals from 20,000 km away: it is jammable and spoofable close to a contested coast, and most of what separates one satellite generation from the next is the effort to answer that. Block IIR — “replenishment”, built by Lockheed Martin and launched between 1997 and 2004 — carries the legacy signals only: the civil C/A code on L1 and the encrypted military P(Y) code on L1 and L2, with on-board clock monitoring and a 7.5-year design life. This one is Block IIR flight 2, space vehicle number SVN 43, last assigned pseudo-random-noise code PRN 13 in plane A, slot 5 of the constellation. It was withdrawn from the active constellation on 24 April 2026 — NAVCEN's notice to Navstar users 2026038 — and is now held as an on-orbit spare rather than broadcasting a usable navigation signal.

The U.S. Space Force's 2nd Space Operations Squadron flies it as at least 24 slots in six equally spaced orbital planes at about 20,200 km, each satellite circling the Earth twice a day, with several extra spacecraft aloft so that coverage survives maintenance and decommissioning. For a maritime operator the point to hold onto is that this is a one-way broadcast of very weak signals from 20,000 km away: it is jammable and spoofable close to a contested coast, and most of what separates one satellite generation from the next is the effort to answer that. Block IIR-M — “modernised”, launched between 2005 and 2009 — added the second civil signal L2C and the military M-code, the jam-resistant signal with flexible transmit power that makes GPS usable in an electronic-warfare environment. This one is Block IIR-M flight 3, space vehicle number SVN 58, broadcasting pseudo-random-noise code PRN 12 in plane B, slot 4 of the constellation.

@us/grace-fo-1/43476.purpose: GRACE-FO 1 is the leading spacecraft of a NASA and German GFZ pair that flies in formation and continuously measures the distance between the two by microwave ranging, with a laser interferometer carried as a technology demonstration. Neither satellite means anything on its own: the measurement is the changing separation, and tiny variations in it map month-to-month shifts in Earth's gravity field, which translate into groundwater, ice sheet and ocean mass change. Launched May 2018 and active, continuing the record GRACE began in 2002.
