@us/gravitas/68495.purpose: K2 Space's first full-scale demonstration of its Gravitas bus, a roughly 2,000 kg flat-bed satellite whose wide planar structure carries very large solar arrays spanning about 40 m deployed, generating up to about 20 kW. It hosts roughly a dozen customer modules, including United States Department of Defense payloads, and flies a 20 kW-class electric thruster. @us/hbtss-sv1/58960.purpose: One of two Hypersonic and Ballistic Tracking Space Sensor prototypes flown for the Missile Defense Agency. Hypersonic glide vehicles are dimmer and manoeuvre unpredictably, so wide-field overhead-persistent-infrared sensors see the launch but cannot hold a track good enough to shoot at. HBTSS carries a narrower, far more sensitive medium-field-of-view infrared sensor in low Earth orbit that takes a cue from the wide-field layer and produces fire-control quality track. SV1 is the L3Harris-built vehicle, since used in MDA and Navy tests against live hypersonic events.

@us/hubble-6/64562.purpose: A 16U cubesat, callsign Lilo, flying Hubble Network's payload to demonstrate direct Bluetooth links between ordinary ground devices and a satellite, so that low-power trackers and sensors can report without cellular coverage. It is a roughly 22 kg spacecraft with a propulsion system for limited station-keeping and collision avoidance, launched with its twin on the Transporter-14 rideshare as a step towards an operational constellation.

@us/hubble-7/64592.purpose: Hubble 7, named Stitch, is a 16U CubeSat of about 22 kg flown for Hubble Network, a company building a satellite network that ordinary Bluetooth-equipped devices on the ground can reach directly without cellular coverage. It flew as one of a pair with Hubble 6 to demonstrate that link, and carries modest propulsion for limited station-keeping and collision avoidance. Earlier Hubble payloads were hosted on Spire Lemur-2 satellites; this generation is a dedicated platform.

@us/icesat-2/43613.purpose: ICESat-2 carries ATLAS, a photon-counting laser altimeter that fires 10,000 pulses a second and times the return of individual photons. From that it measures ice sheet and glacier elevation, sea ice freeboard — the height of floating ice above the waterline, from which thickness is inferred — and also land elevation and forest canopy height. It is a NASA mission launched in September 2018 and is still active.

@us/ico-g-1/32763.organization: ICO Satellite Management -> DBSD North America -> EchoStar
@us/ico-g-1/32763.purpose: A Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300S mobile satellite services spacecraft in the 2 GHz band, one of only two such FCC licences issued, designed to work with an Ancillary Terrestrial Component so that satellite and cellular coverage could be combined across the United States. It replaced ICO's earlier plan for a twelve-satellite medium-Earth-orbit constellation. The operator became DBSD North America in 2009 and the satellite passed to DISH in 2012 as EchoStar G1.

@us/ihopsat-td/44859.purpose: 1HOPSat TD, a 12U CubeSat technology demonstrator flown by Hera Systems of San Jose to prototype a planned eight-satellite commercial imaging constellation. It carried an imaging telescope for roughly one-metre ground sample distance stills and video, downlinked over an X-band OQPSK link, with an experimental C-band command channel and an Iridium short-burst-data backup. It had no propulsion, and catalogue records indicate operations ended within a few months of launch.

@us/image/26113.purpose: IMAGE was the first mission built to photograph Earth's magnetosphere as a whole rather than sample it point by point, using energetic neutral atom imaging together with ultraviolet imaging and radio sounding to watch the ring current, plasmasphere and aurora react to the solar wind. NASA lost contact on 18 December 2005, most probably a single-event upset in the spacecraft's power controller. An amateur observer picked up its carrier again in January 2018 and NASA confirmed the identification, but it has not returned to service.

@us/impulse-1-mira/58301.purpose: Impulse Space's first Mira orbital transfer vehicle, flown as the LEO Express-1 mission. Driven by eight 22 N Saiph bipropellant thrusters, it carried out eight burns over four months including a large orbit raise, a plane change and a debris-avoidance manoeuvre prompted by a US Space Force conjunction warning, and delivered a 3U TrustPoint navigation CubeSat to a custom orbit. Impulse ended active operations in July 2024 after returning the vehicle to a parking orbit.

@us/impulse-2-mira/62673.purpose: Impulse Space's second Mira orbital transfer vehicle, flown as LEO Express-2. Mira is a free-flying, chemically propelled tug: it separates from the launch vehicle, then manoeuvres to place customer payloads into orbits the rideshare itself does not reach, or hosts them for on-orbit operations. It uses the company's Saiph thruster. For an operator, this is the class of vehicle that decouples a smallsat's final orbit from the rideshare drop-off orbit.

@us/impulse-3-mira/66687.purpose: Impulse 3, the third flight of Impulse Space's Mira orbital transfer vehicle, flown on the Transporter-15 rideshare under the LEO Express service name. Mira is a free-flying, chemically propelled tug that carries cubesat deployers and hosted payloads and manoeuvres them from the rideshare drop-off orbit to a customer orbit. Earlier Mira vehicles were used with Starfish Space to fly a camera-only rendezvous demonstration that closed to about 1.2 km between two of them.

@us/ixpe/49954.purpose: IXPE, the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer, measures the polarisation of X-rays — the orientation of the light's electric field — which carries information about magnetic field geometry and source shape that brightness and spectrum alone cannot give. It observes magnetars, pulsars, supernova remnants, black hole jets and active galactic nuclei. Flown by NASA with Italian Space Agency participation, it launched in December 2021 into a near-equatorial low orbit and remains active.

@us/jackal-004/69012.purpose: Jackal is True Anomaly's autonomous orbital vehicle: a manoeuvrable spacecraft built to close on another object, image it and hold station, with flexible payload accommodation. This is the fourth to fly. The first two, launched in 2024, reached orbit and deployed, but the company lost contact with one and never received telemetry from the other. The line is aimed at military space-domain awareness and on-orbit inspection rather than at any remote-sensing product.

@us/jackal-01/59127.purpose: Jackal X-1L-001, the first of two autonomous orbital vehicles flown by True Anomaly of Centennial, Colorado, built to demonstrate live and simulated rendezvous and proximity operations with flexible payloads and high manoeuvrability - the commercial end of space domain awareness and on-orbit inspection. Both vehicles reached orbit, but contact with this one was established and then lost, and the company could not command either spacecraft, so the demonstration objectives went unmet.

@us/jackal-02/59134.purpose: The second of True Anomaly's first two Jackal autonomous orbital vehicles, roughly 275 kg spacecraft built in Centennial, Colorado for rendezvous and proximity operations: closing on another satellite and imaging it for inspection, test and operator training. On this Mission X flight both vehicles powered up and deployed their solar arrays, but True Anomaly lost communications with them and the planned rendezvous between the pair was never carried out.

@us/jason-3/41240.purpose: Jason-3 measures sea surface height by radar altimetry, continuing without a gap the precision record that began with TOPEX/Poseidon in 1992. It is run jointly by NOAA, NASA, CNES and EUMETSAT. For an operator the altimetry is not only sea level: the height field reveals eddies and boundary currents, and the ocean heat content inferred from it feeds directly into hurricane intensity forecasting, wave and tide forecasting for shipping, and El Nino monitoring. Launched January 2016 and still operational.

@us/jupiter-3-echostar-24/57479.purpose: Hughes's Ultra High Density Satellite: a multi-spot-beam Ka-band spacecraft built by Maxar on the SSL-1300 bus with an entirely new payload architecture - miniaturised electronics, solid-state amplifiers and more efficient antennas - reaching about 500 Gbps of throughput concentrated where demand is highest. At roughly 9,200 kg it is among the largest commercial communications satellites ever launched and required a Falcon Heavy. It has a twenty-year design life.

@us/kestrel-0a/64624.purpose: An experimental HawkEye 360 satellite, also called Block 3 Lite, built on a UTIAS Space Flight Laboratory 8U CubeSat bus and launched on Electron with the Hawk 12 cluster. It operates inside the licensed HawkEye 360 constellation, which monitors and geolocates terrestrial radio-frequency emitters from low Earth orbit for maritime domain awareness and interference detection. Kestrel-0A adds an Iridium transceiver giving low-rate, near-real-time two-way contact between ground-station passes.

@us/lcs-1/1361.purpose: Lincoln Calibration Sphere 1 is a hollow aluminium sphere 1.12 metres across with a 3.2 mm wall, made by Rohr Corp. for MIT Lincoln Laboratory and launched in 1965. A sphere returns the same radar echo from every aspect angle, and this one was built so that echo corresponds to exactly one square metre, making it a fixed known reference for calibrating ground radars. It is completely inert, is still used for that purpose, and its orbit is high enough to last on the order of tens of thousands of years.

@us/ldpe-2/54219.purpose: A Long Duration Propulsive ESPA — Northrop Grumman's ESPAStar, which takes the standard secondary-payload adapter ring and adds solar panels, computers, hydrazine thrusters and command-and-control, turning a piece of launch hardware into a manoeuvring free-flyer that hosts up to six payloads or releases up to twelve. Space Systems Command uses it as a freight train to geostationary orbit for prototypes that could never justify their own launch. LDPE-2 flew on USSF-44, the first Falcon Heavy national-security mission, hosting a communications experiment, a commercial-parts maturation payload and a space-weather sensor, and releasing the two LINUSS servicing cubesats, Millennium's Alpine and the TETRA-1 pathfinder.

@us/leo-1/43113.purpose: Telesat LEO 1, also called LEO Vantage 1: a 168 kg Ka-band high-throughput prototype built by Surrey Satellite Technology on the SSTL-42 bus, one of two demonstrators Telesat ordered in 2016 to test and validate the design of its planned global low-Earth-orbit broadband constellation, later named Lightspeed. It flew as a co-passenger on an Indian PSLV-XL. It is a technology pathfinder, not operational capacity.

@us/les-5/2866.purpose: LES 5, the fifth Lincoln Experimental Satellite, was built by MIT Lincoln Laboratory under the tri-service Tactical Satellite Communications programme so the Army, Navy and Air Force could evaluate military UHF satellite links from ships, aircraft and mobile ground terminals. It also carried solar cell degradation and radio frequency interference experiments. It was deactivated in May 1971 — and in early 2020, nearly 49 years later, observers found it emitting telemetry again.

@us/lime/62648.purpose: NOVI's first satellite mission, launched on SpaceX Transporter-12, flown to qualify the company's SP240 on-board computer and edge processor in orbit. NOVI describes LIME as having established flight heritage for that computer and as having run several successful on-orbit experiments including communications and on-board algorithms and machine learning. The aim of the product line is to process sensor data on the spacecraft and downlink only the results, cutting bandwidth and latency.

@us/link/69792.purpose: Link is the servicing vehicle of Katalyst Space Technologies' Swift Rescue Mission, built to rendezvous with NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and raise its decaying orbit before atmospheric drag brings the twenty-year-old gamma-ray burst observatory down. Swift was never designed to be captured, so Link must approach, inspect and grapple a non-cooperative target using a mechanism that attaches to structure rather than instruments, then impart reboost thrust without overloading the spacecraft.

@us/linuss1/55246.purpose: One of a pair of Lockheed Martin In-space Upgrade Satellite System demonstrators — 12U-class cubesats released near the geosynchronous belt to show that a small, cheap spacecraft can approach, inspect and eventually service or upgrade a large one already on orbit. Between them the pair exercised rendezvous and proximity manoeuvres using low-toxicity propulsion and machine vision, miniaturised space-domain-awareness sensing, high-performance onboard processing, and Lockheed's SmartSat architecture for reloading spacecraft software in flight. They were carried to near-GEO by the LDPE-2 rideshare stack on USSF-44.

@us/linuss2/55247.purpose: The second of Lockheed Martin's two In-space Upgrade Satellite System demonstrators, released near the geosynchronous belt to show that a small, cheap spacecraft can approach, inspect and eventually service or upgrade a large one already on orbit. The two vehicles operated as a pair: one manoeuvres relative to the other, exercising rendezvous and proximity operations with low-toxicity propulsion and machine vision while carrying miniaturised space-domain-awareness sensing, high-performance onboard processing and Lockheed's SmartSat architecture for reloading spacecraft software in flight. Both were carried to near-GEO by the LDPE-2 rideshare stack on USSF-44.

@us/lizziesat-2/62383.purpose: The second LizzieSat, and the flight with a documented payload set: Exo-Space's FeatherEdge onboard processing unit for image analysis in orbit, and a Simera Sense HyperScape100 imager operated under NOAA remote-sensing licence at roughly 3.8 m ground sampling. It flies in a mid-inclination rather than sun-synchronous plane, trading consistent lighting for more frequent revisit over the mid and low latitudes.

@us/lizziesat-3-ls-3/63233.purpose: The third LizzieSat, returning to a sun-synchronous plane after the mid-inclination second flight. Sidus Space builds these as a serial product line rather than as one-off spacecraft, the long-term aim being a large constellation spanning inclinations from about 28 to 98 degrees for near-real-time Earth observation and IoT collection. Gunter's Space Page does not list LS-3's specific payloads, and none are asserted here.

@us/lizziesat/59132.purpose: The first of Sidus Space's LizzieSat line, a hybrid, largely 3D-printed multi-mission smallsat built in Merritt Island, Florida. The platform is the product: a reconfigurable bus intended to carry mixed Earth observation and IoT payloads for different customers on each flight, with onboard processing. Gunter's Space Page does not itemise LizzieSat-1's payload complement, and this write-up does not assert one.

@us/lmrst-sat/40971.purpose: A 3U CubeSat from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory carrying the Low Mass Radio Science Transponder, a stripped-down two-way X-band Doppler and ranging unit derived from Deep Space Network navigation practice. The point was to raise the technology readiness of a transponder small enough for deep-space smallsats, supporting not only navigation but gravity-field determination and radio-occultation profiling of planetary atmospheres. It flew on NASA's ELaNa-12 mission with a Pumpkin CubeSat bus.

@us/lopen/60473.purpose: A 1.5U CubeSat flown by Array Labs of Palo Alto, coated on every external surface with an experimental surface treatment. An otherwise identical uncoated counterpart flies as the control, and the divergence between the two orbital decay curves is the measurement: a direct in-orbit test of whether a surface coating meaningfully changes aerodynamic drag on a small satellite. It carries no propulsion and no other payload.

@us/lynk-tower-3/55046.purpose: A Lynk Global satellite built to work as a cell tower in orbit: it presents itself to an ordinary unmodified mobile handset as a terrestrial base station, so subscribers get messaging and basic connectivity outside any terrestrial network without new hardware. Lynk holds the first commercial licences issued for satellite direct-to-standard-phone service. The trade is coverage over capacity, a fast-moving satellite serves each cell only briefly.

@us/lynk-tower-4/55034.purpose: A Lynk Global direct-to-device satellite flown with Lynk Tower 3. Lynk's approach differs from a conventional satellite phone: no special terminal is used, the spacecraft emulates a standard mobile network cell so that ordinary handsets attach to it. Lynk partners with terrestrial mobile network operators rather than competing with them, and its service targets messaging, IoT and emergency communications in places with no terrestrial coverage.

@us/lynk-tower-5/59121.purpose: The fifth Lynk Tower satellite, flown as a pair with Lynk Tower 6. Each spacecraft is a small orbiting base station serving unmodified phones on standard cellular frequencies licensed from the terrestrial operator it partners with. The constellation's usefulness scales with the number of satellites: with a handful in orbit, service is intermittent store-and-forward messaging rather than continuous connectivity.

@us/lynk-tower-6/59123.purpose: The sixth Lynk Tower satellite, launched alongside Lynk Tower 5. Each is an orbiting base station that appears to an unmodified handset as an ordinary cell, using spectrum licensed from the terrestrial operator Lynk partners with. Lynk has since been granted commercial direct-to-device authority covering US Pacific territories including Guam, which matters operationally: a standard phone ashore can reach a network with no terrestrial infrastructure surviving beneath it.

@us/m-sel/63231.purpose: MITRE's Space Experimentation Lab satellite, also called Cortez: a roughly 40 kg spacecraft on an Astro Digital Corvus-Micro bus carrying a MITRE-built radio-frequency payload. It tests the Frequency-scaled Ultrawide Spectrum Element antenna, an aperture intended to work across several widely separated bands at once, and exercises multi-band RF communications on orbit. It is a technology experiment rather than an operational communications asset.

@us/makersat-0/43016.purpose: A 1U cubesat from Northwest Nazarene University in Nampa, Idaho, built with NearSpace Launch and flown on NASA's ELaNa-14 rideshare with the JPSS-1 weather satellite. Its structure is 3D printed, and its four science boards expose different additive-manufacturing polymers to vacuum, atomic oxygen and ultraviolet so their mass loss can be tracked from orbit; it also carries a camera. It was the precursor to MakerSat-1, which was printed and assembled aboard the ISS.

@us/mandrake-2-able/48907.purpose: One of two Mandrake 2 satellites flown as risk reduction for DARPA's Blackjack programme, which set out to show that a proliferated constellation of cheap commercial-bus satellites in low Earth orbit could do work previously reserved for a few large, expensive spacecraft. Able and Baker carried SA Photonics optical inter-satellite link terminals on Astro Digital buses built in about nine months, testing the laser crosslinks a meshed LEO network needs to move data without touching a ground station.

@us/mandrake-2-baker/48908.purpose: The second of two Mandrake 2 satellites flown as risk reduction for DARPA's Blackjack programme, which argued that cheap commercial-bus satellites in low Earth orbit could do work previously reserved for a few large spacecraft. Baker and its twin Able carried SA Photonics optical inter-satellite link terminals on Astro Digital buses, testing the laser crosslinks a meshed LEO network needs. Both were damaged when a deployer was accidentally triggered before Transporter-1 and flew on Transporter-2 instead.

@us/mcubed-2/39469.purpose: M-Cubed/COVE-2, a 1U CubeSat from the University of Michigan's Student Space Systems Fabrication Lab, reflying a mission that failed when the first M-Cubed magnetically latched onto another CubeSat immediately after deployment. It carries a camera for roughly 200-metre-resolution Earth imagery together with JPL's CubeSat On-board processing Validation Experiment, which tested onboard processing to cut the data rate of a multi-angle spectropolarimetric imager by two orders of magnitude.

@us/mercury-one-m1/66742.purpose: Proteus Space's first spacecraft: an ESPA-class bus carrying four hosted payloads from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, UC Davis and Leonardo DRS, flown under a SpaceWERX and AFRL Space Vehicles Directorate contract. The mission's real subject is the design process rather than the payloads. Proteus took the vehicle from blank sheet to launch in about nine months using its automated concurrent-engineering platform, adding the Leonardo DRS radio payload after preliminary design review.

@us/meson-1/59131.purpose: Catalogued as Meson, this object is Atomos Space's Quark-Lite orbital transfer vehicle, renamed before flight, launched with its target spacecraft Gluon on the Transporter-10 rideshare as the Singing Astronomer demonstration. The pair were to rendezvous, dock autonomously, transfer propellant and then perform further release, propulsive and orbital-transfer manoeuvres, proving building blocks for Atomos's planned space-resident tugs offering orbit raising, life extension and cargo delivery.

@us/mev-1/44625.purpose: MEV-1 is the first Mission Extension Vehicle, operated by SpaceLogistics, a Northrop Grumman company. It docked with Intelsat 901 in February 2020 — the first docking of two commercial spacecraft in orbit — and then supplied that satellite's station keeping and attitude control from its own thrusters and propellant, letting a fuel-exhausted but otherwise healthy satellite keep earning. It does not refuel the client; it clamps on and flies the stack. It completed the five-year contract in 2025 and moved to a further client.

@us/mev-2/46113.purpose: MEV-2 is the second SpaceLogistics Mission Extension Vehicle. Launched in August 2020, it rendezvoused and docked with Intelsat 10-02 in April 2021 — this time with the client satellite still in its operational geostationary slot, rather than moving it to a graveyard orbit for the approach. As with MEV-1 there is no refuelling: the servicer supplies the propulsion and pointing itself, so the pair is flown as a single stack for the length of the contract.

@us/minxss-2/43758.purpose: The second Miniature X-ray Solar Spectrometer, a 3U cubesat built by the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder on a Blue Canyon bus and flown on the SSO-A rideshare. It measures the soft X-ray spectrum of the Sun from about 0.4 to 30 keV at roughly 0.15 keV resolution, the band that drives ionospheric response during flares. The first unit flew from the ISS and reentered in 2017; this one was placed directly into a sun-synchronous orbit.

@us/misr-c-1/68628.purpose: MISR-C 1 is a 16U CubeSat flown by US Special Operations Command, the third generation of its Modular Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance experiments after the MISR-A and MISR-B satellites. It is an experiment rather than a programme of record: the stated aims are responsive, multi-mission capability, testing two-way communications directly with ground devices, and exploring tactical uses for small satellites. Reference sources assess the payload as signals-intelligence related but do not confirm it.

@us/misr-c-2/68633.purpose: The second Modular Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance CubeSat, a 16U spacecraft flown by US Special Operations Command on a Minotaur IV rideshare with STPSat-7. It is described as demonstrating responsive multi-mission smallsat capability, including two-way communication with handheld ground devices and novel tactical applications of small satellites for special operations forces. Published assessments suggest a signals-intelligence payload, but that has not been confirmed by the operator.

@us/misr-d-1/69908.organization: Apex Space (operator reported as US Special Operations Command)
@us/misr-d-1/69908.purpose: Also catalogued as Flashpoint 1, a roughly 100 kg satellite built by Apex Space on its Aries bus and flown as one of a pair. It is described as a responsive multi-mission demonstrator testing two-way communications with ground devices and novel tactical uses of small satellites, with a signals-intelligence element. Which organisation actually operates it is not firmly established in public sources.

@us/misr-d-2/69915.purpose: MISR-D 2, also called Flashpoint 2, an experimental satellite for United States Special Operations Command built by Apex on its Aries platform. The MISR-D pair are intended to demonstrate responsive, multi-mission small satellites for tactical users, including two-way communication with ground devices and novel tactical applications of smallsats. The sensing payload is assessed as signals intelligence but has not been publicly described by the operator.

@us/mola/59289.purpose: A 6U CubeSat built and operated by the Naval Postgraduate School's Space Systems Academic Group in Monterey, flown on the NRO's NROL-123 Electron launch. It carries an NPS-built terahertz imaging camera; LOOP, a bank of nine ultra-bright 527 nm green LEDs that let a ground telescope see the satellite optically, a first step toward optical tracking and free-space laser links that sidestep congested radio bands; and Korimako, a transmitter from New Zealand's Defence Science and Technology group. It is run through the Five Eyes MC3 ground station network.

@us/momentus-x1/44408.purpose: El Camino Real, a 16U cubesat built by Astro Digital to flight-test Momentus's water-based microwave electrothermal thruster, the propulsion intended for the company's Vigoride transfer vehicles. It flew as a secondary payload on a Soyuz launch. Momentus initially reported success, but a later SEC filing showed the mission missed its objectives: against a target of 100 firings of at least a minute, no firing reached that duration and only three of 23 attempts produced plasma, and contact was lost after three months.

@us/monolith/49052.purpose: An AFRL technology demonstrator carrying a space-weather instrument package on a deployable boom, launched by Rocket Lab from New Zealand on the Space Test Program's STP-27RM mission. The experiment is really about structural dynamics rather than space weather: the deployed sensor accounts for a large fraction of the whole spacecraft's mass, which shifts its moments of inertia, and the question is whether a small bus can still hold attitude with a big aperture hanging off it. If it can, future deployable-sensor missions — weather satellites among them — can fly on cheaper buses and shorter timelines.

@us/mtg-s1/64723.purpose: MTG-S1 is the first Meteosat Third Generation sounder and Europe's first geostationary sounding satellite, operated by EUMETSAT with ESA. Its Infrared Sounder builds vertical profiles of temperature and humidity over Europe, Africa and the surrounding oceans far more often than a polar-orbiting sounder can, which is what buys lead time on fast-developing convection. It also carries the Copernicus Sentinel-4 ultraviolet-visible-near-infrared instrument for air quality and trace gases. Launched 1 July 2025; commissioning closed in July 2026.

@us/musat2/59099.purpose: Muon Space's second spacecraft and its first operational sensing mission, a roughly 67 kg satellite carrying a polarimetric GNSS reflectometry payload. GNSS-R reads navigation signals bounced off the sea surface: the roughness of the reflection gives surface wind speed, and over land the same technique gives soil moisture. Because it uses signals of opportunity rather than a transmitter, it works through the heavy rain that blinds conventional scatterometers, which is exactly the tropical cyclone core case.

@us/musat3/64573.purpose: Catalogued as MuSat 3 but flown as VanZyl-2, Hydrosat's second thermal infrared satellite, built on Muon Space's Condor-M Halo platform with thermal and multispectral instruments from ABB and Simera Sense. It measures land surface temperature, from which evapotranspiration and crop water stress are derived; the same thermal signal supports drought and wildfire work. Hydrosat states it carries about four times the collection capacity of VanZyl-1.

@us/n2-p-body/69929.purpose: P-Body is one of the first satellites of NOVI's GENIEedge constellation, a 6U CubeSat offered as shared, taskable orbital infrastructure rather than as an imagery product: customers buy fractional use of its sensing and computing. Each spacecraft carries a visible camera at roughly 3 metre ground sampling, a 96-band hyperspectral and near-infrared imager at about 35 metres, and a software-defined radio receiver spanning 47 MHz to 6 GHz, with onboard processing so results can be downlinked instead of raw data.

@us/nanoace/42844.purpose: A 3U CubeSat flown by Tyvak Nano-Satellite Systems purely for internal development, validating the company's Endeavour command and data handling, guidance and control software and actuators before committing them to customer missions. It carried two infrared and two visible cameras with onboard image processing, and a VACCO cold-gas thruster set, and was used to demonstrate three-axis pointing at various targets and small propulsive manoeuvres.

@us/npsat1/44340.purpose: An 86 kg microsatellite designed and built by students and faculty at the Naval Postgraduate School in Monterey, flown as a secondary payload on the Air Force STP-2 mission. It carries a solar-cell measurement system, a configurable fault-tolerant processor, a visible-wavelength imager, and two Naval Research Laboratory space-weather instruments: a CERTO radio beacon for ionospheric tomography and a Langmuir probe. Roughly forty student theses fed into it; education was the primary objective.

@us/nts-3/65160.purpose: Navigation Technology Satellite 3, AFRL's experimental GEO testbed for resilient positioning, navigation and timing, and the first US navigation technology demonstrator since NTS-2 helped prove GPS in 1977. An electronically steerable phased array broadcasts Earth-coverage and spot beams at once, and a reprogrammable on-orbit digital waveform generator lets operators upload new signals, authentication and anti-jam waveforms after launch. The operational point is disaggregation: PNT that does not depend solely on GPS, with a beam that can be steered at a jammed theatre. Built by L3Harris on an ESPAStar bus.

@us/nustar/38358.purpose: NuSTAR was the first orbiting telescope able to focus hard X-rays rather than merely collect them. Its grazing-incidence optics sit at the end of a mast extended after launch, which is what supplies the focal length in a small spacecraft. NASA uses it to study black hole populations, neutron stars, supernova remnants and the most extreme active galaxies, and it made the first precise measurement of a black hole's spin. Launched June 2012 and still active.

@us/o-oreos-usa-219/37224.purpose: O/OREOS — Organism/Organic Exposure to Orbital Stresses — was NASA Ames Research Center's first astrobiology nanosatellite, a triple CubeSat flown as a secondary payload on the Space Test Program's STP-S26 mission. One module, SESLO, rehydrated dormant bacteria in orbit and measured their growth and survival; the other, SEVO, exposed thin films of astrobiologically significant organic molecules to solar ultraviolet and trapped-particle radiation and tracked their breakdown by spectroscopy. The experiments concluded in May 2011.

@us/oco-2/40059.purpose: OCO-2 measures carbon dioxide by taking high-resolution spectra of reflected sunlight, returning the column-averaged dry-air mole fraction at the precision needed to see where CO2 is taken up and released at the surface. The same spectra also yield solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence, a direct optical measure of photosynthesis. It is a NASA mission in a sun-synchronous orbit, launched in July 2014, and remains active.

@us/omni-l1/52157.purpose: Catalogued as OMNI-L1 but flown as Spark-1, the first of Omnispace's two S-band pathfinders for a planned hybrid satellite and terrestrial mobile network built to 3GPP standards. The spacecraft is a NanoAvionics smallsat carrying an S-band payload from Thales Alenia Space with Syrlinks, exercising a narrowband IoT radio interface direct from orbit, the non-terrestrial network approach in which the satellite is simply another cell of a standards-based mobile network.

@us/omni-l2/52771.purpose: Spark-2, the companion to OMNI-L1 in Omnispace's S-band demonstration pair. Omnispace holds global S-band mobile-satellite spectrum rights and is using these two spacecraft to prove a direct-to-device narrowband IoT service that behaves as part of a standard 3GPP network rather than as a separate satellite system. Both are NanoAvionics platforms with a Thales Alenia Space S-band payload.

@us/ops-5712-p-l-153/2874.purpose: Catalogued under the cover designation OPS 5712, this object is Naval Research Laboratory payload 153 — one of four Poppy 5 satellites launched together on 31 May 1967. Poppy was NRL's electronic intelligence system, run inside NRO Program C, which located Soviet air and missile defence radars by comparing the arrival time of the same signal at several satellites at once. The programme was declassified in 2005; its later clusters added ship tracking and became the prototypes for the Navy's ocean surveillance satellites.

@us/ops-5712-p-l-160/2826.purpose: Catalogued under the cover designation OPS 5712, this object is Naval Research Laboratory payload 160, a passive calibration sphere launched on 31 May 1967 with four Poppy electronic-intelligence satellites and the first Timation navigation experiment. It has no power, no sensors and no transmitter. Its job was to give the Naval Space Surveillance fence and other radars a target whose size and radar cross-section were known exactly, so that what was being measured was the sensor rather than the target.

@us/opticube-04/41851.purpose: A completely passive 2U CubeSat built by Cal Poly as an on-orbit calibration target. It carries no payload, power or transmitter; ground optical and radar sensors observe it as an object of precisely known size, shape and surface coating so that orbital-debris measurement systems can be calibrated and small-object tracking validated. The OptiCube units differ only in exterior coating material. It was produced at short notice for the NASA Orbital Debris Program Office and the Air Force Starfire Optical Range.

@us/orbiter-sn3/56960.purpose: An Orbiter free-flying deployer built by Launcher and flown on the Transporter-8 rideshare, sized to carry up to 400 kg with roughly 500 m/s of delta-v from ethane and nitrous oxide propulsion. Shortly after separation a software fault sent it into an uncontrollable spin, its solar panels could not hold power, and its payloads were released early - successfully, but into the rideshare orbit. It therefore could not serve as the docking target for Starfish Space's Otter Pup. Launcher was acquired by Vast and the Orbiter programme was cancelled.

@us/oresat0-5/60525.organization: Portland State Aerospace Society, Portland State University
@us/oresat0-5/60525.purpose: OreSat0.5 is a 1.5U CubeSat of about 2 kg from the Portland State Aerospace Society at Portland State University, flown to qualify the attitude determination and control system of the OreSat bus. OreSat is a modular, expandable and fully open-source CubeSat design whose hardware and software are published for reuse by other student programmes, so this flight is best read as a bus-qualification step rather than as a mission with its own science payload.

@us/ors-5-sensorsat/42921.purpose: SensorSat, flown as ORS-5 by the Operationally Responsive Space Office as a low-cost gap-filler between SBSS and its successor. MIT Lincoln Laboratory built the 140 kg spacecraft and gave it an unusual answer to a hard problem: rather than slewing a gimbaled telescope, it flies in a near-equatorial orbit at essentially zero inclination and lets the geosynchronous belt sweep past a fixed sensor, scanning the whole GEO ring for uncatalogued objects and manoeuvres. Launched on a Minotaur-4 in August 2017, it demonstrated that a small, cheap satellite can hold a useful share of the space-surveillance mission.

@us/oscar-7/7530.purpose: AMSAT-OSCAR 7 is an amateur radio satellite built by volunteers and launched in November 1974, carrying linear transponders that relay amateur signals across a continent-sized footprint. Its batteries failed in 1981 and it fell silent; in June 2002, after 21 years, it was heard again, apparently because a failed cell went open circuit and let the spacecraft run straight off its solar panels. It therefore works only in sunlight, and it is the oldest satellite of any kind still in service.

@us/otb/44341.purpose: Orbital Test Bed 1, a 138 kg SSTL-150 class satellite whose business is renting room to hosted payloads, letting customers qualify hardware in orbit without buying a dedicated mission. It was built by Surrey Satellite Technology and is operated by General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems, which acquired SSTL's US assets in 2017. Its best-known passenger was NASA's Deep Space Atomic Clock, a miniature mercury-ion clock for autonomous deep-space navigation.

@us/otp-2/63235.purpose: An 11 kg CubeSat flown by Rogue Space Systems of Laconia, New Hampshire as an orbital test platform. Its job is to shake out the company's avionics stack in flight: onboard computing hardware, sensor aggregation, and algorithms that process data in place rather than downlinking raw measurements, alongside space for hosted third-party experiments. Published sources disagree on whether the structure is 6U or 8U.

@us/otter-pup-2/64537.purpose: Starfish Space's second Otter Pup, a roughly 40 kg satellite-servicing demonstrator flown on the Transporter-14 rideshare. It exercises the three technologies needed for the company's full-size Otter servicer: the Nautilus electrostatic capture mechanism, the Cephalopod guidance and control software, and the Cetacean relative-navigation software, using a Redwire Argus camera for relative navigation. The first Otter Pup could not complete its docking demonstration because its intended target, Launcher's Orbiter SN3, tumbled after deployment.

@us/otter-sdm/66678.purpose: OTTER — Optical Traffic Tracking Experiment for Responsive Space — is a 3U CubeSat of DLR, the German aerospace centre, and despite the name has nothing to do with Starfish Space's Otter servicing vehicles. It demonstrates CubeLCT, a miniaturised laser communications terminal derived from DLR's OSIRIS programme and commercialised with Tesat-Spacecom: about 0.3U, 350 grams, and roughly 100 Mbit/s space-to-ground. UHF is used for routine command and control while the optical link is tested.

@us/otter/62623.purpose: A 6U CubeSat built and operated by the Naval Postgraduate School, the US Navy's graduate institution, deployed from the January 2025 Transporter-12 rideshare. It has no propulsion and is catalogued as a technology demonstration, but the specific experiment it carries is not described in any public source located in this session. Treat it as an NPS technology-demonstration CubeSat of undocumented payload rather than an operational asset.

@us/pace-1/48909.purpose: A 6U CubeSat from NASA's Ames Research Center flying the agency's Payload Accelerator for CubeSat Endeavors, a programme meant to shorten the path from bench prototype to flight-qualified smallsat technology. It demonstrates a modular avionics core built largely from commercial parts, including a switching scheme that lets several GPS and radio systems share one antenna and so free up surface area, and it hosts four additional technology payloads.

@us/pace/58928.purpose: PACE — Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem — carries the hyperspectral Ocean Color Instrument together with two polarimeters, SPEXone and HARP2. Hyperspectral ocean colour lets it distinguish phytoplankton communities rather than just total chlorophyll, while the polarimeters characterise aerosol particle size and type and how aerosols seed and modify cloud. It is a NASA mission launched in February 2024 into a sun-synchronous orbit and is active.

@us/palisade/44634.purpose: A 40 kg, 16U CubeSat built and operated by Astro Digital of Mountain View as a technology demonstrator for its Corvus product line: an onboard propulsion system, a next-generation communications payload and flight software from Advanced Solutions Inc. Rocket Lab flew it alone on the As The Crow Flies Electron mission and placed it above 1,000 km, higher than any previous Electron flight had reached.

@us/pandora/67395.purpose: NASA's Pandora, the first satellite of the Astrophysics Pioneers programme, led by Goddard Space Flight Center with project management from Lawrence Livermore. It studies transiting exoplanet atmospheres, and its particular job is to fix the error that limits the field: a star's own spots and bright regions imprint a signal on a transit spectrum that mimics planetary chemistry. Pandora observes visible and near-infrared light simultaneously, through a 45 cm all-aluminium telescope and a spare James Webb detector, so the stellar contribution can be separated out. Year one covers at least twenty known planets.

@us/pathfinder-1/41787.purpose: BlackSky Pathfinder-1, the first demonstrator for BlackSky's commercial imaging constellation, built by Spaceflight Services on its SCOUT bus with a 24 cm-aperture SpaceView-24 imager from Exelis, giving roughly one-metre ground resolution and up to about twenty stills per day in four bands. It performed well enough that its twin, Pathfinder-2, was never launched and BlackSky moved directly to operational satellites. It flew as a secondary payload on India's PSLV.

@us/pcsat/26931.purpose: PCsat, also Navy-OSCAR 44, is a 10 kg satellite built by midshipmen at the US Naval Academy, funded by the Academy and Boeing and launched through the DoD Space Test Program. It works as an orbiting digipeater for the Automatic Packet Reporting System, relaying short position and text packets from handheld and mobile stations that are nowhere near terrestrial infrastructure — Academy sailboats at sea, expeditions, remote travellers — into the worldwide internet-linked APRS network via volunteer ground stations.

@us/pe2-flt1-tyvak-0261/59105.purpose: Pony Express 2A, catalogued as Tyvak-0261: one of two identical 12U cubesats funded and built by Tyvak to raise the readiness of Lockheed Martin RF payloads for crosslink, ranging and receive experiments. The pair flew together on Transporter-10 and operate in the same orbit a few kilometres apart to demonstrate satellite-to-satellite networking, precision timing and Lockheed's SmartSat software-defined payload architecture. Each is about 26 kg and uses a ThrustMe iodine ion thruster.

@us/pe2-flt2-tyvak-0262/59104.organization: Tyvak Nano-Satellite Systems with Lockheed Martin
@us/pe2-flt2-tyvak-0262/59104.purpose: Pony Express 2B is the second of a pair of 26 kg, 12U CubeSats funded and built by Tyvak carrying radio-frequency payloads developed by Lockheed Martin. The two fly in near-identical orbits three to five kilometres apart to demonstrate satellite-to-satellite crosslinks, precision ranging and timing, and onboard analytics under Lockheed's SmartSat software-defined architecture — groundwork for autonomous teaming and cloud-style networking between spacecraft. An iodine ion thruster provides orbit control.

@us/pelican-1-3001/58296.purpose: A Planet Labs Pelican, the high-resolution tasking line now succeeding SkySat. Pelican-1 is not an imaging satellite in the operational sense: launched in November 2023, it was the platform technology demonstration that qualified the bus, avionics and on-orbit compute before Planet committed to the Gen-1 production run. Planet's own documentation begins the operational Gen-1 series with Pelican-3, treating Pelican-1 and Pelican-2 as precursors.

@us/pelican-11/69871.purpose: A Planet Labs Pelican, the high-resolution tasking line now succeeding SkySat. Pelican-11 is a dedicated engineering pathfinder rather than a production imager. Launched on Transporter-17 in July 2026, it flies the technologies intended for the Gen-2 Pelicans, which are designed for 30 cm class imagery against Gen-1's 50 cm - so it is the satellite to watch for what the constellation will look like next, not for imagery today.

@us/pelican-2-3009/62631.purpose: A Planet Labs Pelican, the high-resolution tasking line now succeeding SkySat. Gen-1 Pelicans carry a 4 m focal-length Cassegrain telescope with dual panchromatic arrays and six multispectral bands for 50 cm class imagery, and an NVIDIA Jetson processor that screens scenes on orbit so the time from tasking to delivered image runs in hours rather than a day. Pelican-2 is the first to carry the imaging payload, launched January 2025, with first light over the Port of Laem Chabang, Thailand; its band set differs slightly from the Gen-1 satellites that followed.

@us/pelican-3-300a/65315.purpose: A Planet Labs Pelican, the high-resolution tasking line now succeeding SkySat. Gen-1 Pelicans carry a 4 m focal-length Cassegrain telescope with dual panchromatic arrays and six multispectral bands for 50 cm class imagery, and an NVIDIA Jetson processor that screens scenes on orbit so the time from tasking to delivered image runs in hours rather than a day. Pelican-3 opens the operational Gen-1 series in Planet's own documentation. It launched in August 2025 with Pelican-4 and returned its first light over Turin, Italy, a fortnight later, while still climbing to its final operating orbit.

@us/pelican-4-300b/65316.purpose: A Planet Labs Pelican, the high-resolution tasking line now succeeding SkySat. Gen-1 Pelicans carry a 4 m focal-length Cassegrain telescope with dual panchromatic arrays and six multispectral bands for 50 cm class imagery, and an NVIDIA Jetson processor that screens scenes on orbit so the time from tasking to delivered image runs in hours rather than a day. Pelican-4 launched on the same Falcon 9 as Pelican-3 in August 2025, the pair that began commercial Gen-1 operations; its six bands are matched to Planet's PlanetScope Doves so wide-area and high-resolution tasking can be analysed together.

@us/pelican-5-300c/66667.purpose: A Planet Labs Pelican, the high-resolution tasking line now succeeding SkySat. Gen-1 Pelicans carry a 4 m focal-length Cassegrain telescope with dual panchromatic arrays and six multispectral bands for 50 cm class imagery, and an NVIDIA Jetson processor that screens scenes on orbit so the time from tasking to delivered image runs in hours rather than a day. Pelican-5 launched with Pelican-6 on the Transporter-15 rideshare in November 2025, alongside a batch of SuperDoves - a single flight that reinforced both the tasking and the wide-area sides of Planet's fleet.

@us/pelican-6-300d/66703.purpose: A Planet Labs Pelican, the high-resolution tasking line now succeeding SkySat. Gen-1 Pelicans carry a 4 m focal-length Cassegrain telescope with dual panchromatic arrays and six multispectral bands for 50 cm class imagery, and an NVIDIA Jetson processor that screens scenes on orbit so the time from tasking to delivered image runs in hours rather than a day. Pelican-6 achieved first light the day after its November 2025 launch, imaging Lhasa Gonggar airport in Tibet; the speed of that turnaround is itself the point of the on-orbit processing the Gen-1 design carries.

@us/pelican-7-300e/69017.purpose: A Planet Labs Pelican, the high-resolution tasking line now succeeding SkySat. Gen-1 Pelicans carry a 4 m focal-length Cassegrain telescope with dual panchromatic arrays and six multispectral bands for 50 cm class imagery, and an NVIDIA Jetson processor that screens scenes on orbit so the time from tasking to delivered image runs in hours rather than a day. Pelican-7 launched in May 2026 with Pelicans 8 and 9. Its launch mate Pelican-8 became Sweden's first sovereign satellite, run by the Swedish Armed Forces - allied ministries now buy national capacity off a commercial line.

@us/pelican-9-3010/69019.purpose: A Planet Labs Pelican, the high-resolution tasking line now succeeding SkySat. Gen-1 Pelicans carry a 4 m focal-length Cassegrain telescope with dual panchromatic arrays and six multispectral bands for 50 cm class imagery, and an NVIDIA Jetson processor that screens scenes on orbit so the time from tasking to delivered image runs in hours rather than a day. Pelican-9 is the third of the May 2026 trio; with that launch nine AI-enabled Pelicans were on orbit against a planned constellation of thirty-two.

@us/pext/64874.purpose: Bard, a 140 kg York Space Systems microsatellite carrying the Polylingual Experimental Terminal, built by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory for NASA's Space Communications and Navigation programme. Its wideband software-defined radios switch between frequency bands, waveforms and relay providers on the fly, so a spacecraft can move between NASA's TDRSS relays, commercial relay networks and a direct-to-Earth path. It is groundwork for NASA's planned move to commercial relay services.

@us/podsat/43229.purpose: A DARPA-sponsored demonstration of NovaWurks' satlet architecture: small modular cells that pool power, data and thermal capacity and can be aggregated into spacecraft of arbitrary size. Four HISat cells were integrated into a chassis built by SSL, carried to orbit attached to the Hispasat 30W-6 communications satellite and released after the primary separated. It is the deployable element of DARPA's Payload Orbital Delivery programme, built to exploit spare launch capacity.

@us/polar-scout-yukon/43808.organization: DHS Science and Technology Directorate / U.S. Coast Guard
@us/polar-scout-yukon/43808.purpose: One of the two Polar Scout 6U cubesats, Yukon and Kodiak, flown by the DHS Science and Technology Directorate with the Coast Guard to test whether cheap smallsats can detect and geolocate 406 MHz emergency distress beacons over Arctic waters. The driver was a coverage gap: the MEOSAR search-and-rescue constellation was years from full capability while Arctic maritime activity grew. The pair were tracked from a five-site S-band ground network including Fairbanks and New London, and exercised against Arctic test beacons through 2019.

@us/polar/23802.purpose: Polar was the second spacecraft of NASA's Global Geospace Science programme within the International Solar-Terrestrial Physics campaign. From a high-inclination elliptical orbit it imaged the northern aurora in visible, ultraviolet and X-ray light while its particle, field and wave instruments measured the plasma along the same track, which is how energy entering the dayside cusp and crossing the polar cap was tied to what the aurora actually showed. Launched in February 1996, it was retired on 28 April 2008.

@us/popacs-2/39269.organization: POPACS collaboration (Utah State University, Drexel University, Planetary Systems Corp.)
@us/popacs-2/39269.purpose: The middle of three identical 10 cm aluminium spheres flown together as POPACS, a university-led project directed by Gil Moore. The spheres are sand-ballasted to 1, 1.5 and 2 kg so that identical drag surfaces give different ballistic coefficients and separate in the orbit over time. Radars and student observers track their divergent decay to measure how upper-atmosphere density responds to solar flares and coronal mass ejections. The spheres are entirely passive, with no power or transmitter.

@us/popacs-3/39270.organization: POPACS consortium (Utah State University, Drexel University, Planetary Systems Corporation)
@us/popacs-3/39270.purpose: One of three Polar Orbiting Passive Atmospheric Calibration Spheres, released together from a 3U dispenser on the Falcon 9 v1.1 CASSIOPE launch. Each is a hollow 10 cm sphere loaded with sand to a different mass - 1, 1.5 and 2 kg - so that three identical shapes with different ballistic coefficients decay at different rates from the same orbit. Tracking their divergence measures how upper-atmosphere density responds to solar activity. They are entirely passive: no power, no radio, no attitude control.

@us/prefire-1/59965.purpose: PREFIRE-1 is one of two CubeSats carrying a miniature spectrometer that measures the far-infrared part of Earth's outgoing radiation — the wavelengths that carry much of the heat the polar regions shed to space, and which had never been measured systematically from orbit. Two spacecraft in different orbit planes revisit the same scene at varying intervals, which is how the changes are caught. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory manages the mission with the principal investigator at the University of Wisconsin-Madison; it launched in 2024 and has been extended.

@us/prefire-2/59881.purpose: PREFIRE-2 is one of two CubeSats carrying a miniature spectrometer that measures the far-infrared part of Earth's outgoing radiation — the wavelengths that carry much of the heat the polar regions shed to space, and which had never been measured systematically from orbit. @us/propcube-1/40976.purpose: A 1U CubeSat from the Naval Postgraduate School, built on a Tyvak bus, and an unusual kind of instrument: the satellite is the transmitter and the measurement happens on the ground. It radiates dual-frequency beacons to receivers including Arecibo and HAARP, and the differential delay between the two frequencies gives total electron content while amplitude and phase scintillation reveal plasma irregularities — the ionospheric conditions that degrade GPS and HF. It can also detect artificial ionisation deliberately produced by the HAARP, Arecibo and Sura heating facilities. This unit is named Flora.

@us/propcube-3/40973.purpose: A 1U CubeSat from the Naval Postgraduate School, built on a Tyvak bus, and an unusual kind of instrument: the satellite is the transmitter and the measurement happens on the ground. @us/proves-electra/69799.purpose: PROVES-Electra is a 1U CubeSat from the University of California Santa Cruz, built on the PROVES kit — the Pleiades Rapid Orbital Verification Experimental System that Cal Poly Pomona's Bronco Space developed on the PyCubed architecture and publishes open-source so other university programmes can start from a working spacecraft. It reached orbit by being carried to the International Space Station and deployed from it, which is why it carries a 1998-067 designator rather than one from its own launch.

@us/prox-1/44339.purpose: A 71 kg Georgia Tech student-built spacecraft, winner of the seventh Air Force University Nanosat Program competition. It was to fly automated proximity operations around The Planetary Society's LightSail 2 using passive imaging for relative orbit determination, but software problems forced a 2017 descope that stripped out the propulsion, sensors and solar cells. It flew as a battery-powered optical calibration target and successfully deployed LightSail 2 on the STP-2 mission.

@us/ptd-4/60565.purpose: A 6U CubeSat in NASA's Pathfinder Technology Demonstrator series, managed by Ames Research Center and built by Terran Orbital. Its payload is LISA-T, a thin-film deployable solar array with an integrated antenna developed at Marshall Space Flight Center, offering roughly three times the power per unit mass and volume of conventional rigid arrays. A central boom pushes four stowed petals about a metre clear of the bus before they unfurl; the design scales from about 100 to 500 watts.

@us/pulsar-0/64541.purpose: Xona Space Systems' first operational-class Pulsar satellite, built by Aerospacelab, demonstrating a commercial low-Earth-orbit alternative and augmentation to GPS. From LEO it broadcasts navigation signals far stronger than legacy GNSS, with signal authentication intended to defeat spoofing and corrections aimed at sub-decimetre positioning. It carries no propulsion, traded away to fly sooner. For operators it is the leading example of the LEO-PNT approach to jamming and spoofing resilience.

@us/punch-nfi00/63178.purpose: PUNCH-NFI00 carries the Narrow Field Imager, the coronagraph of NASA's four-satellite PUNCH constellation. It blocks the solar disk and images the inner corona in polarised white light, covering the region where the corona stops being a bound atmosphere and becomes the solar wind — the transition no earlier mission imaged continuously. Polarisation is what makes the picture three-dimensional, because it encodes how far material lies from the plane of the sky. Launched in March 2025; science operations began that June.

@us/punch-wfi01/63179.purpose: PUNCH-WFI01 carries one of the three Wide Field Imagers of NASA's PUNCH constellation. Each WFI covers roughly 44 degrees of sky; the three of them, together with the coronagraph on the fourth spacecraft, are operated synchronously as a single virtual instrument more than 90 degrees wide centred on the Sun. That continuous field is what lets a coronal mass ejection be tracked in polarised white light from the corona out past Earth's orbit instead of being lost between instruments. Launched March 2025 and operating.

@us/punch-wfi02/63181.purpose: PUNCH-WFI02 carries one of the three Wide Field Imagers of NASA's PUNCH constellation. @us/r5-s2/60207.purpose: A 6U cubesat from NASA's Johnson Space Center, flown as R5 S2-2.0 on a Firefly Alpha launch, testing whether commercial off-the-shelf cameras, computers and algorithms are good enough for free-flying external inspection of crewed spacecraft. It is among the first of the R5 series to carry cold-gas nitrogen reaction control, which is what makes controlled stand-off inspection rather than passive drift possible. The aim is a low-cost inspector that can be sent to look at a vehicle rather than sending a crew member outside.

@us/r5-s4/60206.purpose: R5-S4 is a 6U CubeSat from NASA's Johnson Space Center, one of a pair flown to assess whether commercial off-the-shelf cameras, processors and vision algorithms are good enough for free-flying external inspection of crewed vehicles and stations — work otherwise done by spacewalks or robotic arms. It and its twin were the first in the R5 series to carry cold-gas nitrogen reaction-control propulsion, giving them the manoeuvring needed to fly around a target.

@us/r5-s9/69901.purpose: One of NASA Johnson Space Center's R5-series CubeSats, a deliberately low-cost line that tests whether commercial off-the-shelf cameras, computers and algorithms are good enough for free-flying external inspection of crewed vehicles - work aimed at making crewed exploration safer and cheaper. Later members of the series are 6U spacecraft fitted with cold-gas nitrogen thrusters. Catalogues disagree about which piece of this crowded rideshare launch carries the R5-S9 identity.

@us/range-a/43773.purpose: One of a pair of identical 1.5U CubeSats from Georgia Tech's Space Systems Design Laboratory, flown in leader-follower formation to improve the absolute and relative positioning of nanosatellites. Each carries a GPS receiver disciplined by a miniature atomic clock, retroreflectors for ground-based laser ranging, and a compact onboard laser ranging unit that doubles as a low-rate optical link. With no propulsion, separation between the two was controlled by differential drag.

@us/raptor1/58957.purpose: One of the last four Tranche 0 Tracking Layer satellites, built by L3Harris on a Moog bus for the Space Development Agency, carrying a wide-field-of-view overhead persistent infrared sensor to detect and track ballistic and hypersonic missiles from low orbit. It shares a 40-degree orbit with the two HBTSS spacecraft launched with it on USSF-124 by design: SDA's wide-field sensor and MDA's narrower fire-control sensor can watch the same test article at the same time, which is how the cue-and-handoff chain gets proven. This launch completed Tranche 0 at twenty-seven satellites on orbit.
