@us/ravan/41849.organization: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory
@us/ravan/41849.purpose: A 3U CubeSat led by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory on a Blue Canyon XB1 bus, funded by NASA and flown under the CubeSat Launch Initiative. It demonstrated two technologies for measuring Earth's radiation imbalance: a broadband radiometer whose absorber is a forest of vertically aligned carbon nanotubes, and gallium fixed-point blackbodies used as a stable on-orbit calibration reference. It began collecting Earth radiation data in January 2017 and met all mission objectives that August.

@us/rawhide-1/68629.organization: U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command
@us/rawhide-1/68629.purpose: The first of two Rawhide cubesats flown for the US Army Space and Missile Defense Command on a Minotaur IV alongside STPSat-7, continuing SMDC's long-running line of small satellites that develop and transition tactical space support concepts directly to ground forces. Its 60-degree inclination is unusual for a smallsat and gives repeated coverage of mid-latitudes rather than the sun-synchronous global sweep typical of rideshare cubesats. No payload details have been released.

@us/rawhide-2/68632.organization: U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command
@us/rawhide-2/68632.purpose: Rawhide 2 is a 6U-class CubeSat of the US Army Space and Missile Defense Command, flown as one of a pair of secondary payloads on the Space Test Program's STP-S29A Minotaur IV launch alongside STPSat-7. SMDC's small-satellite line has historically pursued beyond-line-of-sight tactical communications — relaying voice, text and ground-sensor data to deployed radios, as the SMDC-ONE nanosatellites did. The Rawhide payload itself has not been publicly described.

@us/ray-1-0/62627.purpose: A small reentry capsule with an attached service module, built by Inversion Space of Long Beach, California, as a scaled precursor to its larger Arc vehicle intended to hold cargo in orbit and return it on demand. Ray 1.0 completed its on-orbit checkout of key technologies during a mission planned to last about four weeks, but never attempted reentry: a short circuit in one component stopped the deorbit engine igniting.

@us/real/64875.purpose: Relativistic Electron Atmospheric Loss: a 3U CubeSat led by Dartmouth College with Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, Boston University and Montana State University, flown under NASA's CubeSat Launch Initiative. Its particle detector points along the local magnetic field line and measures the energy and pitch angle of electrons scattering out of the Van Allen belts into the atmosphere, the loss process that sets how long relativistic electron populations persist after a geomagnetic storm.

@us/rigidsphere-2-lcs-4/5398.purpose: Despite the name it carries in the catalogue, this is Lincoln Calibration Sphere 4: a hollow aluminium sphere built for MIT Lincoln Laboratory and launched on 7 August 1971 with a group of Space Test Program payloads. It is entirely passive — no power, no instruments, no transmitter — and exists so ground radars can be checked against an object whose radar cross-section is precisely known and identical from every direction. It is still used for that. It is not a missile-warning or early-warning satellite.

@us/rock/60474.purpose: One half of a two-satellite drag experiment by Array Labs. Rock and Lopen are near-identical 1.5U CubeSats of about 1.8 kg; Lopen carries a novel retroreflective surface coating meant to increase drag largely independent of attitude or tumble rate, and Rock flies uncoated as the experimental control. Comparing the two decay rates isolates the coating's effect. Results feed the design of Array Labs' planned Earth imaging constellation.

@us/rroci-2/59106.purpose: EWS-RROCI 2, a rebuild of the Rapid Revisit Optical Cloud Imager prototype for the US Space Force's Electro-Optical/Infrared Weather System. It is a roughly 18 kg 12U cubesat carrying an eight-channel EO/IR imager built by Orion Space Solutions with Lockheed Martin, Science and Technology Corporation, Pumpkin and Atmospheric and Environmental Research, intended to characterise global cloud cover in near real time for theatre weather support. The first RROCI never deployed from its launch vehicle and reentered with the upper stage, so this replacement was built on an expedited schedule.

@us/runner-1-tyvak-1005/56953.purpose: Runner 1 is an 86 kg optical imaging satellite operated by ImageSat International and built by Tyvak on Terran Orbital's avionics platform, carrying ImageSat's electro-optical mission system. Its 35 centimetre telescope returns true-colour stills and video at roughly 71 centimetre ground resolution over a 5.6 kilometre swath, sold to commercial and government intelligence customers. It doubles as FASat-Delta for the Chilean Air Force, which procured it through an international tender for Chile's national space programme.

@us/s5/44065.purpose: A 60 kg AFRL space-situational-awareness microsatellite built on a Blue Canyon bus, flown to test whether cheap small satellites stationed inside the geostationary belt could detect and locate near-GEO objects and keep the GEO catalogue refreshed far more often than ground sensors manage. It launched as a co-passenger on a commercial GEO mission. It then went silent: AFRL had no contact after March 2019, and the agency later used its Mycroft experimental satellite to fly out and inspect S5 on orbit — a first-of-its-kind anomaly-resolution rendezvous, and a practical demonstration of why inspection capability matters.

@us/sal-e/68458.organization: Cal Poly CubeSat Laboratory (PolySat), California Polytechnic State University
@us/sal-e/68458.purpose: A 3U CubeSat from the student-run CubeSat Laboratory at California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, named in honour of astronaut Sally Ride. It is primarily an education platform, run by volunteer students across design, assembly, test, launch preparation and operations. Two payloads ride along: a microchip evaluated as a novel radiation sensor, and a receive-only radio that demonstrates a new communications device while monitoring the 902 to 915 MHz band.

@us/satgus/62713.purpose: A 12U CubeSat funded by CrunchLabs, the education company founded by former NASA engineer Mark Rober, and built on a Terran Orbital / Tyvak bus. Its payload is a Google Pixel phone facing a camera: a user uploads a selfie, the phone displays it, and the satellite photographs the screen with Earth behind it. The purpose is public engagement rather than research, though the spacecraft itself is fully functional.

@us/sbss-usa-216/37168.purpose: Space Based Space Surveillance Block 10, the pathfinder that gave the Space Surveillance Network its first dedicated orbital optical sensor. A 30 cm visible-band telescope on a two-axis gimbal slews between targets without turning the spacecraft, and from low Earth orbit it watches the geosynchronous belt free of the weather, daylight and atmospheric limits that constrain ground telescopes, producing position, manoeuvre-detection and object-identification data on satellites and debris. Boeing was prime with Ball supplying bus and telescope; it reached full operational capability in 2013 and outlived its seven-year design life.

@us/sdo/36395.purpose: The Solar Dynamics Observatory watches the Sun without interruption from an inclined geosynchronous orbit, chosen so a single dedicated ground station can take its very high data rate continuously. It images the solar atmosphere in many extreme-ultraviolet channels, maps the photospheric magnetic field and the flows beneath the surface, and measures the Sun's extreme-ultraviolet irradiance — the input that heats and expands the thermosphere and so drives satellite drag. Launched in February 2010, it is still operating.

@us/seahawk-1/43820.purpose: A 3U CubeSat built by AAC Clyde Space and led by the University of North Carolina Wilmington with NASA Goddard, funded by the Moore Foundation under the Sustained Ocean Color Observations with Nanosatellites project. Its HawkEye sensor imaged ocean colour in eight spectral bands at about 120 m ground resolution, far finer than heritage SeaWiFS, over open ocean, coasts, estuaries and lakes. It returned over 9,000 NASA-archived scenes before being decommissioned after five years.

@us/sedna-1/60580.purpose: A 4U cubesat built and operated by AAC SpaceQuest carrying a space-based Automatic Identification System receiver, extending the company's S-AIS infrastructure and validating new maritime space-data technologies. Space-based AIS picks up the self-reporting transmissions of ships far beyond coastal receiver range, and is a standard input to maritime domain awareness. This spacecraft reached its orbit as a payload carried on a D-Orbit ION transfer vehicle rather than by direct separation from the launch vehicle.

@us/sedna-2/63153.purpose: Sedna-2 is a 4U CubeSat built and operated by AAC Clyde Space's SpaceQuest business to receive maritime Automatic Identification System broadcasts from orbit. Ships transmit AIS over VHF for local collision avoidance; collecting those transmissions from space extends ship tracking across open ocean far beyond the reach of coastal receivers. The satellite exists both to add capacity to the company's satellite-AIS service and to validate new maritime space-data technologies.

@us/sert3/68499.purpose: A technology demonstration satellite operated by Muon Space of Mountain View, California, flown on the company's Condor-class small-satellite bus. Public information is unusually sparse for a US commercial spacecraft: the operator has published no mission page, and the identification rests on independent catalogue entries that agree only on the operator, the bus and a technology-demonstration classification. The payload and its purpose should be treated as unestablished.

@us/ses-3/37748.purpose: An Orbital Sciences Star-2.4 hybrid satellite ordered by SES Americom as the ground spare of a multi-satellite contract and renamed SES 3 in 2010. It carries 24 active C-band and 24 Ku-band transponders of 36 MHz each, some cross-strapped between bands, plus a small Ka-band capability, with two deployable reflectors and about five kilowatts of payload power. It was launched by a Proton-M/Briz-M.

@us/sherpa-ac1/52763.purpose: The first Sherpa-AC, Spaceflight Inc's free-flying rideshare tug, adding a flight computer, attitude determination and control, power and RF to the basic Sherpa dispenser. Beyond releasing customer satellites it hosts payloads in low Earth orbit for up to a year; on this flight it carried Xona Space Systems' Huginn navigation-signal demonstrator and NearSpace Launch's TROOP-3 telemetry unit, which remains attached for years.

@us/sherpa-fx2-tagsat-2/48958.purpose: The Sherpa-FX2 free-flying deployer from SpaceX's Transporter-2 rideshare, catalogued together with its hosted TagSat-2 payload. Sherpa-FX carries no propulsion or attitude control; it expands the number of rideshare ports, releases its customer spacecraft, here including Lynk, Hawk, Astrocast, Lemur-2 and SpaceBEE satellites, then remains in orbit as an inert structure. TagSat-2, from NearSpace Launch and later renamed TROOP-2, stays attached and provides continuous telemetry for hosted experiments.

@us/sherpa-ltc2/53754.purpose: A Sherpa-LTC free-flying space tug from Spaceflight Inc., flown not as a deployer but as a dedicated host for Boeing's Varuna technology demonstration mission. Its Benchmark Polaris propulsion burns high-test peroxide and isopropyl alcohol through four independently commanded 22 N thrusters, so it steers without a gimbal. Released from a Starlink launch into a low orbit, it raised itself towards an operational orbit near 1050 km to test V-band propagation and terminal performance for Boeing's proposed non-geostationary broadband constellation.

@us/sinod-d-1/40974.purpose: A 2U CubeSat from SRI International — the name stands for SRI International NanoSat Orbital Demonstration — built on a Tyvak bus to demonstrate a high-speed downlink for wide-bandwidth CubeSat payloads using software-defined radio. It is a communications technology demonstration rather than a science mission: the bottleneck for a small satellite carrying a capable sensor is usually getting the data down, and a reprogrammable radio is the flexible way to attack it. The identification of this particular object is contested between catalogues.

@us/sinod-d-3/40977.purpose: A 2U CubeSat from SRI International — the name stands for SRI International NanoSat Orbital Demonstration — built on a Tyvak bus to demonstrate a high-speed downlink for wide-bandwidth CubeSat payloads using software-defined radio. It is a communications technology demonstration rather than a science mission: the bottleneck for a small satellite carrying a capable sensor is usually getting the data down, and a reprogrammable radio is the flexible way to attack it. Unlike its sibling, this object's catalogue identity is not disputed.

@us/sirion-pathfinder-2/43759.purpose: Sirion Pathfinder 2, also catalogued as Helios Wire Pathfinder 2, is a 6U CubeSat built by Astro Digital as a demonstrator for a planned S-band machine-to-machine and Internet-of-Things constellation. It carries an Enpulsion field-emission electric propulsion unit for orbit control. It flew on Spaceflight Industries' SSO-A dedicated rideshare, the mission that first showed a US commercial broker could fill an entire Falcon 9 with small satellites. Sirion Global was acquired by EchoStar Global in 2019.

@us/sirius-fm-5/35493.purpose: The first geostationary satellite in the Sirius satellite radio system. Built by Space Systems/Loral on the SSL-1300 bus, it carries an X-band uplink and S-band downlink digital audio radio payload feeding a nine-metre unfurlable reflector, which concentrates enough power that ordinary car and portable receivers work without a dish. With more than 20 kW end-of-life power it was among the most powerful commercial satellites built. It supplements the three original Sirius satellites in highly inclined elliptical orbits.

@us/sirius-fm-6/39360.purpose: Near-identical to Sirius FM-5 on the Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300 bus, but built to broadcast in both the Sirius and the XM frequency allocations after the two companies merged. It was originally ordered for a highly inclined elliptical orbit to replace Sirius FM-1 and FM-2, then instead placed in geostationary orbit at 116.15 degrees West. Same X-band uplink, S-band downlink digital audio radio payload with a large unfurlable reflector.

@us/sirius-xm-10/64290.purpose: SXM-10, one of the third-generation SiriusXM digital audio radio satellites built by Maxar on the SSL-1300 bus. Like its siblings it broadcasts in S-band, generates more than 20 kW and carries a large unfurlable antenna reflector so that subscribers' vehicle and portable radios need no dish. Ordered in August 2021 alongside SXM-9 as part of the fleet renewal that followed the loss of SXM-7. It was launched by a Falcon 9.

@us/sirius-xm-11/69728.purpose: SXM-11, the newest of SiriusXM's third-generation digital audio radio satellites, ordered from Maxar in November 2022 together with SXM-12 and built on the SSL-1300 bus. It carries the same S-band broadcast payload and large unfurlable reflector as the rest of the series, sustaining nationwide satellite radio coverage as the second-generation XM and Sirius spacecraft age out. Launched by a Falcon 9 in June 2026.

@us/sirius-xm-9/62259.purpose: SXM-9, ordered from Maxar in August 2021 specifically as the replacement for SXM-7, which failed in orbit. A third-generation SiriusXM digital audio radio satellite on the SSL-1300 bus with an S-band payload, more than 20 kW of power and a large unfurlable antenna reflector that lets ordinary car radios receive the signal directly. It was launched by a Falcon 9 from Kennedy Space Center.

@us/skysat-1/39418.purpose: SkySat-1 is the original of the line: an 83 kg satellite built in-house by Skybox Imaging in 2013, before Google bought the company and before Planet acquired it, and the spacecraft that demonstrated that sub-metre stills and short high-definition video could come off a smallsat rather than a bus-sized imaging platform. It is a Generation-A vehicle, not one of the later SSL-built SkySat-C production satellites.

@us/skysat-2/40072.purpose: SkySat-2 is the second and last Generation-A satellite, launched from Baikonur on a Soyuz in 2014 while the company was still Skybox Imaging. It shares the 3.6 m focal-length Ritchey-Chretien telescope and CMOS focal plane of SkySat-1, whose native resolution at nadir is around 1.1 m - coarser than the 50 cm product the later production fleet delivers.

@us/skysat-c1/41601.purpose: A Planet Labs SkySat, one of the tasking satellites that return 50 cm imagery and 30-120 second video clips of a commanded point rather than wide-area coverage. The useful property for a watch floor is responsiveness: the fleet can revisit a given position several times a day, and it images what an operator asks for. C1 is the first modernised Generation-C production satellite - about 120 kg, built by SSL to a Skybox-licensed design, with green-propellant thrusters the prototypes lacked. It launched alone on a PSLV in 2016, under Google's Terra Bella.

@us/skysat-c10/42988.purpose: A Planet Labs SkySat, one of the tasking satellites that return 50 cm imagery and 30-120 second video clips of a commanded point rather than wide-area coverage. The useful property for a watch floor is responsiveness: the fleet can revisit a given position several times a day, and it images what an operator asks for. C10 is one of the October 2017 Minotaur-C batch, launched under Planet Labs; its 5.7 km swath means it is a point-target sensor, not an area-search sensor, and must be tasked against a known position.

@us/skysat-c11/42987.purpose: A Planet Labs SkySat, one of the tasking satellites that return 50 cm imagery and 30-120 second video clips of a commanded point rather than wide-area coverage. The useful property for a watch floor is responsiveness: the fleet can revisit a given position several times a day, and it images what an operator asks for. C11 is the last of the six satellites launched together on a Minotaur-C in October 2017, completing the pre-2020 SkySat constellation that Planet later lowered from about 500 km to 450 km to improve resolution.

@us/skysat-c2/41773.purpose: A Planet Labs SkySat, one of the tasking satellites that return 50 cm imagery and 30-120 second video clips of a commanded point rather than wide-area coverage. The useful property for a watch floor is responsiveness: the fleet can revisit a given position several times a day, and it images what an operator asks for. C2 is one of four Generation-C satellites launched together on a Vega from Kourou in September 2016, the first multi-satellite SkySat deployment and the launch that turned the line from a pair of prototypes into a working constellation.

@us/skysat-c3/41774.purpose: A Planet Labs SkySat, one of the tasking satellites that return 50 cm imagery and 30-120 second video clips of a commanded point rather than wide-area coverage. The useful property for a watch floor is responsiveness: the fleet can revisit a given position several times a day, and it images what an operator asks for. C3 is one of the four-satellite Vega batch of September 2016, flown while the fleet still belonged to Terra Bella; Planet acquired it the following year and later lowered the orbits to sharpen the imagery.

@us/skysat-c4/41771.purpose: A Planet Labs SkySat, one of the tasking satellites that return 50 cm imagery and 30-120 second video clips of a commanded point rather than wide-area coverage. The useful property for a watch floor is responsiveness: the fleet can revisit a given position several times a day, and it images what an operator asks for. C4 is one of the September 2016 Vega quartet. Like every Generation-C satellite it carries the ECAPS high-performance green propulsion system that made the 2020 fleet-wide orbit lowering to 50 cm imagery possible.

@us/skysat-c5/41772.purpose: A Planet Labs SkySat, one of the tasking satellites that return 50 cm imagery and 30-120 second video clips of a commanded point rather than wide-area coverage. The useful property for a watch floor is responsiveness: the fleet can revisit a given position several times a day, and it images what an operator asks for. C5 completes the four Generation-C satellites orbited by a single Vega in September 2016 - the launch that took the SkySat fleet from three spacecraft to seven.

@us/skysat-c6/42992.purpose: A Planet Labs SkySat, one of the tasking satellites that return 50 cm imagery and 30-120 second video clips of a commanded point rather than wide-area coverage. The useful property for a watch floor is responsiveness: the fleet can revisit a given position several times a day, and it images what an operator asks for. C6 is one of six SkySats launched together on a Minotaur-C from Vandenberg in October 2017, the first SkySat launch conducted after Planet's acquisition of Terra Bella and the largest single deployment of the line.

@us/skysat-c7/42991.purpose: A Planet Labs SkySat, one of the tasking satellites that return 50 cm imagery and 30-120 second video clips of a commanded point rather than wide-area coverage. The useful property for a watch floor is responsiveness: the fleet can revisit a given position several times a day, and it images what an operator asks for. C7 is one of the six-satellite Minotaur-C batch of October 2017, which doubled the constellation in one flight and gave Planet enough tasking satellites to offer sub-daily revisit commercially.

@us/skysat-c8/42990.purpose: A Planet Labs SkySat, one of the tasking satellites that return 50 cm imagery and 30-120 second video clips of a commanded point rather than wide-area coverage. The useful property for a watch floor is responsiveness: the fleet can revisit a given position several times a day, and it images what an operator asks for. C8 is one of the October 2017 Minotaur-C six. Its imagery is delivered in the same five bands - blue, green, red, near-infrared and panchromatic - as the rest of the fleet, so scenes from different SkySats are directly comparable.

@us/skysat-c9/42989.purpose: A Planet Labs SkySat, one of the tasking satellites that return 50 cm imagery and 30-120 second video clips of a commanded point rather than wide-area coverage. The useful property for a watch floor is responsiveness: the fleet can revisit a given position several times a day, and it images what an operator asks for. C9 is one of the six Generation-C satellites launched on a Minotaur-C in October 2017, flying the standard SkySat payload that can be commanded to collect stills, stereo pairs or video of a single point.

@us/skyterra-1/37218.purpose: A Boeing BSS-702GEM geomobile satellite with a 22-metre unfurlable L-band reflector and a 1.5-metre Ku-band antenna, built for Mobile Satellite Ventures to serve handheld terminals across North America using ground-based beam forming and an Ancillary Terrestrial Component. Reflector deployment initially failed and took several attempts to complete; a strong solar flare knocked the satellite out in March 2012 and it was recovered. The operator became SkyTerra, then LightSquared, then Ligado Networks.

@us/smdc-one-1-2/38759.organization: U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command
@us/smdc-one-1-2/38759.purpose: An SMDC-ONE nanosatellite, Space and Missile Defense Command Operational Nanosatellite Effect, the Army's experiment in whether a 4.5 kg 3U cubesat built quickly and cheaply could give a deployed unit beyond-line-of-sight communications of its own: collect packetised data from unattended ground sensors on each pass, dump it to a ground station inside the same track, and relay voice and text between field radios that cannot see each other. This vehicle is catalogued elsewhere as SMDC-ONE 2.2 'Baker'.

@us/smdc-one-2-3/39474.organization: U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command
@us/smdc-one-2-3/39474.purpose: An SMDC-ONE nanosatellite — Space and Missile Defense Command Operational Nanosatellite Effect — the Army's experiment in whether a 4.5 kg 3U cubesat built quickly and cheaply could give a deployed unit beyond-line-of-sight communications of its own, collecting packetised data from unattended ground sensors on each pass and relaying voice and text between field radios that cannot see each other. This vehicle, COSPAR 2013-072N, is catalogued elsewhere as SMDC-ONE 3.1 'Charlie', released with a cluster of cubesats from the Atlas-5 that carried NROL-39 in December 2013.

@us/snap-3-alice/40970.organization: U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command
@us/snap-3-alice/40970.purpose: SNAP-3 ALICE is one of three 3U CubeSats built for the US Army Space and Missile Defense Command and launched together in October 2015 as rideshares on an NRO mission. The SMDC Nanosatellite Program used software-defined radios to demonstrate beyond-line-of-sight voice and data relay for small units with no other communications path. This generation was the command's first with propulsion, attitude control and deployable solar arrays, and about five times the data rate of the earlier SMDC-ONE satellites.

@us/snap-3-eddie/40972.organization: U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command
@us/snap-3-eddie/40972.purpose: SNAP-3 EDDIE is one of three 3U CubeSats built for the US Army Space and Missile Defense Command and launched together in October 2015 as rideshares on an NRO mission. The SMDC Nanosatellite Program used software-defined radios to demonstrate beyond-line-of-sight voice and data relay for small units with no other communications path. This generation was the command's first with propulsion, attitude control and deployable solar arrays, and about five times the data rate of the earlier SMDC-ONE satellites.

@us/snap-3-jimi/40975.organization: U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command
@us/snap-3-jimi/40975.purpose: SNAP-3 JIMI is one of three 3U CubeSats built for the US Army Space and Missile Defense Command and launched together in October 2015 as rideshares on an NRO mission. The SMDC Nanosatellite Program used software-defined radios to demonstrate beyond-line-of-sight voice and data relay for small units with no other communications path. This generation was the command's first with propulsion, attitude control and deployable solar arrays, and about five times the data rate of the earlier SMDC-ONE satellites.

@us/sorce/27651.organization: NASA / LASP, University of Colorado Boulder
@us/sorce/27651.purpose: SORCE measured how much energy the Sun actually delivers: total solar irradiance from its Total Irradiance Monitor, and the spectrum from about 1 to 2400 nanometres from SIM, SOLSTICE and the XUV Photometer System. The ultraviolet end matters most for this site's subject, because that is the part that varies strongly over a solar cycle and controls heating of the upper atmosphere. Run by LASP at the University of Colorado Boulder, it operated from January 2003 until 25 February 2020, spanning two solar minima.

@us/spacemobile-001/61047.purpose: One of the first five commercial BlueBird satellites, the operational follow-on to the BlueWalker 3 prototype. Each unfolds a phased array of about 693 square feet, the largest commercial array flown in low Earth orbit at the time, and delivers roughly ten times BlueWalker 3's processing bandwidth directly to unmodified smartphones. Five spacecraft give intermittent, not continuous, coverage; AST has demonstrated voice calls over AT&T and Verizon networks using them.

@us/spacemobile-002/61048.purpose: A BlueBird Block 1 satellite from AST SpaceMobile's first commercial batch of five, built at Midland, Texas. The design principle is to put the complexity in space: the array is large enough that an ordinary handset, with its tiny antenna and low transmit power, can close the link unaided. Each satellite supports about 40 MHz of bandwidth and peak rates above 150 Mbps per cell.

@us/spacemobile-003/61045.purpose: One of AST SpaceMobile's five BlueBird Block 1 spacecraft, flown together into a mid-inclination plane that concentrates coverage over populated mid-latitudes rather than the poles. They provide non-continuous service across the United States and selected markets, filling coverage gaps rather than replacing terrestrial networks; continuous global service depends on the far larger Block 2 fleet now being deployed.

@us/spacemobile-004/61049.purpose: A BlueBird Block 1 satellite in AST SpaceMobile's first commercial group of five. AST's model is wholesale: it does not sell directly to subscribers but supplies coverage to mobile network operators using their own licensed spectrum, so the service appears to the user as an extension of their existing carrier. Milestone voice, data and video calls have been demonstrated over these spacecraft in North America, Europe and Japan.

@us/spacemobile-005/61046.purpose: The last of the five BlueBird Block 1 satellites launched together as AST SpaceMobile's first commercial deployment. They are functionally identical repeats of the BlueWalker 3 prototype design, deliberately so, to retire risk before committing to the much larger and more capable Block 2 spacecraft that follow. Large deployable arrays of this kind are also notably bright, a live concern for optical astronomy and for space situational awareness cataloguing.

@us/spacemobile-006/67232.purpose: BlueBird 6, the first BlueBird Block 2 satellite and a step change from the earlier fleet: AST states Block 2 carries up to ten times the bandwidth capacity of Block 1. It was launched not on a US vehicle but on an Indian LVM3, the heaviest payload that rocket had flown, a reminder that commercial direct-to-device constellations procure launch wherever mass and schedule allow.

@us/spacemobile-008/69589.purpose: BlueBird 8, one of three Block 2 satellites launched together on a single Falcon 9. Block 2 BlueBirds are the operational backbone of the SpaceMobile system, designed for continuous rather than intermittent direct-to-handset coverage once enough are in place; AST plans a constellation of up to sixty. Each is substantially larger and higher-capacity than the Block 1 spacecraft it supplements.

@us/spacemobile-009/69590.purpose: BlueBird 9, flown with BlueBirds 8 and 10 on one Falcon 9. Launching Block 2 spacecraft three at a time is what makes the constellation schedule credible: continuous direct-to-phone service requires tens of satellites in the plane, not units, and the rate of deployment rather than the performance of any single spacecraft now sets when the service becomes usable.

@us/spacemobile-010/69591.purpose: BlueBird 10, the third of the Block 2 satellites deployed on a single Falcon 9. AST SpaceMobile builds these largely in-house in Midland, Texas, and operates them wholesale through terrestrial mobile network operators using those operators' licensed spectrum. For an operator ashore or afloat, the practical significance is that a standard handset, not a dedicated satellite terminal, becomes the fallback communications device.

@us/spawar-cal-o/43766.purpose: A 1U Navy calibration target, one of three flown together — passive spacecraft with no active payload whose entire function is to be observed. Ground radars and optical telescopes measure an object whose size, shape and reflective properties are known exactly, and use the difference between what they see and what they should see to calibrate themselves; this is the CubeSat descendant of the 1960s SURCAL satellites. The -O variant carries optical reflectors on all six faces. It is the lowest of the three and will re-enter first.

@us/spawar-cal-or/43778.purpose: A 1U Navy calibration target, one of three flown together — passive spacecraft with no active payload whose entire function is to be observed. Ground radars and optical telescopes measure an object whose properties are known exactly and calibrate themselves against it, as the 1960s SURCAL satellites did. The -OR variant is the interesting one: optical reflectors on three faces and radar reflectors on the other three, so its apparent signature changes with orientation and a sensor can be checked against a target that is not uniform.

@us/spawar-cal-r/43776.purpose: A 1U Navy calibration target, one of three flown together — passive spacecraft with no active payload whose entire function is to be observed. Ground radars and optical telescopes measure an object whose size, shape and reflective properties are known exactly, and calibrate themselves against the difference; this is the CubeSat descendant of the 1960s SURCAL satellites. The -R variant carries radar reflectors on all six faces. It sits highest of the three and will outlast them.

@us/spherex/63182.purpose: SPHEREx surveys the entire sky in optical and near-infrared light, taking a spectrum of every point on it rather than an image through a handful of filters. The survey targets the physics of cosmic inflation, maps water and other ices in the interstellar clouds where planets form, and measures over 450 million galaxies and 100 million Milky Way stars. It launched in March 2025 on the same rocket as the PUNCH constellation and is active.

@us/starcloud-1/66303.purpose: A 60 kg technology demonstrator for Starcloud of Redmond, Washington, built on Astro Digital's Corvus-Micro bus and carrying what its operator describes as the first Nvidia H100 GPU flown in space. It tests high-performance inference and model fine-tuning in orbit as a step toward space-based data-centre services. It was formerly named Lumen 1, entered nominal operations after deployment, and is designed for a short life ending in controlled deorbit.

@us/starling-1/57388.purpose: One of four 6U cubesats making up NASA Starling, a swarm demonstration run by Ames Research Center under the Small Spacecraft Technology programme. The four spacecraft flew as a group to prove the things a swarm needs before it can do science: a mobile ad-hoc radio network linking the satellites by crosslink, autonomous onboard decision-making without ground tasking, optical angles-only navigation to work out where the others are, and autonomous manoeuvre planning. Launched in July 2023, the swarm completed all its primary mission objectives after roughly ten months on orbit.

@us/starling-2/57387.purpose: One of four 6U cubesats making up NASA Starling, a swarm demonstration run by Ames Research Center under the Small Spacecraft Technology programme. The four flew as a group to prove what a swarm needs before it can do science: a mobile ad-hoc radio network, autonomous onboard decision-making without ground tasking, optical angles-only navigation, and autonomous manoeuvre planning. It produced the first autonomous angles-only navigation demonstrated by a satellite swarm.

@us/starling-3/57389.purpose: One of four 6U cubesats making up NASA Starling, a swarm demonstration run by Ames Research Center under the Small Spacecraft Technology programme. The four flew as a group to prove what a swarm needs before it can do science: a mobile ad-hoc radio network, autonomous onboard decision-making without ground tasking, optical angles-only navigation, and autonomous manoeuvre planning. The swarm completed its primary objectives after about ten months; this vehicle now sits in a slightly lower orbit than its companions.

@us/starling-4/57386.purpose: One of four 6U cubesats making up NASA Starling, a swarm demonstration run by Ames Research Center under the Small Spacecraft Technology programme. The four flew as a group to prove what a swarm needs before it can do science: a mobile ad-hoc radio network linking the satellites, autonomous onboard decision-making without ground tasking, optical angles-only navigation, and autonomous manoeuvre planning. The swarm met its primary objectives in about ten months, including reaching consensus on how to observe the ionosphere.

@us/stpsat-5/43762.organization: U.S. Space Force Space Test Program
@us/stpsat-5/43762.purpose: A roughly 115 kg Space Test Program smallsat built by Sierra Nevada Corporation on its SN-50 bus, carrying five experiments for four different agencies — which is what the Space Test Program is for: flying government payloads that have no mission of their own. Aboard were SIRI, a Naval Research Laboratory gamma-ray spectrometer giving europium-doped strontium iodide its first orbital flight; RAMS, an NRL attitude sensor; the Air Force Academy's miniaturised electrostatic analyser for plasma and space-weather data; an AFRL radiation-hardened memory experiment; and HALO-Net, a SPAWAR laser-communications component test.

@us/stpsat-6/49817.organization: U.S. Space Force Space Test Program
@us/stpsat-6/49817.purpose: A 2,500 kg Space Test Program host at geostationary orbit, built by Northrop Grumman on a bus originally procured by DARPA for its Phoenix servicing programme and later transferred to STP. Its best-known passenger is NASA's Laser Communications Relay Demonstration, two 10 cm optical telescopes cross-connected by a switching unit so the satellite works as a genuine relay; it carried the first two-way end-to-end optical relay link with the ISS terminal ILLUMA-T at 1.2 Gbit/s in December 2023. Also aboard is an operational NNSA nuclear-detonation detection payload, plus AFRL, NRL and Air Force Academy space-environment sensors.

@us/stpsat-7/68630.organization: U.S. Space Force Space Test Program
@us/stpsat-7/68630.purpose: An ESPA-class Space Test Program free-flyer built by Aegis Aerospace on its M-1 bus, reusing the bus and ground system first flown on STPSat-4. Three of its five experiments come from the Naval Research Laboratory: LARADO, which detects and characterises orbital debris below about three centimetres that ground radars cannot track; GOSAS, a programmable dual GPS receiver that surveys the orbital GNSS environment and produces ionospheric space-weather products bearing on GPS accuracy and integrity; and GARI-1C, a new gamma-ray detector. It also carries a proliferated-LEO military UHF SATCOM experiment and a satellite fingerprinting security demonstration.

@us/surcal-159/2872.purpose: This is Naval Research Laboratory payload 159, an inert calibration object launched on 31 May 1967 alongside the Poppy 5 intelligence satellites and the first Timation navigation experiment. The Surcal — surveillance calibration — series existed to calibrate the Naval Space Surveillance system, the transmitter and receiver fence strung across the southern United States, by flying targets of known size and known orbit through its beam. Sources disagree over whether this piece is better labelled Surcal or Calsphere; either way it is a passive reference target.

@us/swas/25560.purpose: SWAS, the Submillimeter Wave Astronomy Satellite, was a NASA Small Explorer that observed submillimetre emission lines of water, molecular oxygen, atomic carbon and isotopic carbon monoxide in interstellar clouds, to work out how those clouds shed heat as they collapse into stars. It produced the first survey of how water is distributed through the Milky Way, across more than a hundred molecular clouds. Launched December 1998, it operated until 2005 and was then put into hibernation.

@us/swift/28485.purpose: The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory finds gamma-ray bursts with its wide-field Burst Alert Telescope, then slews within about a minute to put its X-ray and ultraviolet-optical telescopes on the fading afterglow — which is how burst positions reach ground observers while there is still something to see. NASA renamed it for its late principal investigator in 2018. Launched November 2004 and still active, though its orbit has decayed far enough that a commercial reboost mission has been contracted.

@us/swot/54754.purpose: SWOT — Surface Water and Ocean Topography — is a NASA and CNES mission whose KaRIn radar interferometer measures water surface height across a wide swath rather than along a single ground track. That resolves ocean features roughly an order of magnitude finer than earlier altimeters, including the submesoscale eddies and fronts that move heat and momentum vertically, and it gives the first global survey of lakes, reservoirs and river discharge. Launched December 2022 and active.

@us/tacsat-6/39473.organization: U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command
@us/tacsat-6/39473.purpose: A 5 kg 3U cubesat built by the US Army's Space and Missile Defense Command for the Operationally Responsive Space Office, closely related to the Army's SMDC-ONE nanosatellites and flown to demonstrate nanosatellite communications relay. The operational idea behind it was responsiveness: a communications payload that could be re-tasked to a different theatre within about a day to support an unexpected operation, rather than one tied to a fixed regional plan. It was one of twelve secondary payloads released from the Atlas-5 that launched NROL-39 in December 2013.

@us/tanager-1-4001/60507.purpose: Tanager-1 is the first satellite of the Carbon Mapper coalition, a philanthropically funded public-private effort that includes NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Planet Labs, RMI and Arizona State University. Planet built and flies the spacecraft; JPL supplied the imaging spectrometer, which reads over 400 narrow channels between 400 and 2500 nm at about 30 m and identifies methane and carbon-dioxide plumes by their absorption fingerprints. Detections are released publicly thirty days after collection.

@us/tanstaafl-2/62378.purpose: True Anomaly's third Jackal autonomous orbital vehicle, catalogued as Jackal X-2 and also as TANSTAAFL 002. Like its predecessors it is a roughly 275 kg spacecraft built for rendezvous and proximity operations, manoeuvring to and imaging other objects for inspection, test and operator training. It was placed in a mid-inclination orbit on the Bandwagon-2 rideshare rather than the sun-synchronous orbit used by the first two Jackals.

@us/tempsat-1/1512.purpose: Tempsat 1 is a small passive sphere built by the Naval Research Laboratory and launched in August 1965 with the Transit-O 5 navigation satellite and a group of other NRL calibration payloads. The published record describes it as a test of spacecraft thermal control using black paint — the coating that determines how much sunlight a satellite absorbs and how readily it radiates that heat back away, which is the whole of passive thermal design. It has been inert ever since and remains in orbit.

@us/terrestar-1/35496.purpose: A Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300S mobile satellite services spacecraft in the 2 GHz band, carrying a large unfurlable reflector able to generate hundreds of spot beams over the continental United States, Canada, Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, and designed to work alongside a terrestrial Ancillary Terrestrial Component. At about 6,900 kg it was among the heaviest commercial satellites launched to that date. DISH acquired the TerreStar assets in 2012 and renamed it EchoStar T1.

@us/thea/43796.purpose: A 3U CubeSat built by SpaceQuest of Fairfax, Virginia to qualify a proprietary spectrum-survey payload for Aurora Insight, an instrument for characterising the radio-frequency environment from orbit. It also tests a small, low-power VHF backdoor receiver able to command the spacecraft or reboot its flight computer independently of the main TT&C radio, a cheap recovery path for smallsats, and carries an AIS receiver collecting ship position reports. It flew on the SSO-A rideshare.

@us/time-flies/64564.purpose: A TrustPoint technology-demonstration satellite flown on the Transporter-14 rideshare, following the company's first spacecraft, It's About Time. TrustPoint is developing a commercial positioning, navigation and timing service broadcast from low Earth orbit and independent of GPS, and uses these small satellites to mature, calibrate and demonstrate the payload before an operational constellation. LEO PNT is attractive because signals arrive far stronger than from medium-orbit GNSS, which matters where jamming or urban blockage defeats GPS.

@us/timed/26998.organization: NASA / Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory
@us/timed/26998.purpose: TIMED studies the mesosphere and the lower thermosphere-ionosphere, the layer where solar ultraviolet energy is first deposited and where the atmosphere thins into space. That region sets neutral density, and therefore satellite drag and orbit prediction, and it is where the ionosphere that HF and satellite signals must cross is formed. Built and operated for NASA by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, it launched in December 2001 and is still returning data — one of the longest continuous records of the upper atmosphere.

@us/tomorrow-s1/60479.purpose: The first Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder, a 12 kg 6U CubeSat carrying a cross-track scanning passive radiometer descended from the MIT Lincoln Laboratory instrument flown on NASA's TROPICS mission. Its twelve channels, seven oxygen bands near 118 GHz and three water-vapour bands near 183 GHz plus two window channels, retrieve temperature and humidity profiles through cloud across a 2,200 km swath. Sounding from a CubeSat is what makes hourly global revisit affordable.

@us/tomorrow-s10/67398.purpose: The tenth Tomorrow.io microwave sounder, launched into a sun-synchronous plane with S11. Tomorrow.io has stated a target of eighteen sounders in six planes; at this point in the build-out the constellation is dense enough that the interval between soundings of a given tropical system is measured in hours rather than the twice-daily revisit a single polar satellite provides.

@us/tomorrow-s11/67399.purpose: The eleventh Tomorrow.io Microwave Sounder, flown with S10. It is identical to the rest of the series: a 12 kg 6U CubeSat on a Blue Canyon bus carrying a twelve-channel cross-track scanning radiometer operating between roughly 91 and 204 GHz. The lesson for the space cadre is architectural rather than technical, capability that once required a multi-tonne government satellite now arrives as a commercially procured data subscription.

@us/tomorrow-s2/60485.purpose: The second Tomorrow.io microwave sounder, launched with S1 into a sun-synchronous plane. Microwave sounding is the single largest source of forecast skill in global models, and it has historically come from a handful of large government satellites in fixed orbits. A commercial CubeSat constellation attacks the gap between those overpasses, which is where rapidly deepening systems are missed. Tomorrow.io has published sounder imagery of tropical cyclones including Typhoon Yagi.

@us/tomorrow-s3/62392.purpose: The third Tomorrow.io microwave sounder and the first flown into a mid-inclination rather than sun-synchronous plane. That choice is deliberate: a mid-inclination orbit crosses the tropics far more often than a polar one, so the constellation samples the belt where tropical cyclones form at a much shorter interval. The mixed-plane design across six orbital planes is what produces roughly hourly average global revisit.

@us/tomorrow-s4/62386.purpose: A Tomorrow.io microwave sounder flown with S3 into a mid-inclination plane. Each sounder returns temperature and water-vapour profiles at roughly 14 by 17 km at nadir in the high-frequency channels and about 26 by 28 km in the lower ones. Coarse by imager standards, but resolution is not the point: sounders provide vertical thermodynamic structure through cloud, which is what a forecast model actually needs to be initialised.

@us/tomorrow-s5/63234.purpose: The fifth Tomorrow.io microwave sounder, returning to a sun-synchronous plane. The spacecraft bus is a standard Blue Canyon Technologies 6U with a three-year design life; the payload is Tomorrow.io's own build. Latency is a deliberate design goal as much as accuracy, the company delivers products within roughly ten minutes of receiving a downlink, which is what makes commercial sounding data usable in an operational assimilation cycle rather than only in reanalysis.

@us/tomorrow-s6/63225.purpose: A Tomorrow.io microwave sounder launched with S5 into a sun-synchronous plane. The constellation exists to attack the observational hole over ocean: most of the globe has no surface weather observations at all, and passive microwave sounding is the only technique that recovers atmospheric structure through cloud from space. For METOC planners this is the class of commercial data now being bought to supplement, not replace, the government polar sounders.

@us/tomorrow-s7/63631.purpose: The seventh Tomorrow.io microwave sounder, flown singly into a mid-inclination plane at a noticeably higher altitude than the rest of the series. Tomorrow.io's sounders form only half of its Resilience Platform: the other half is the Tomorrow-R Ka-band radar satellites, which actively profile precipitation. Sounders give the thermodynamic environment, the radars give the precipitation structure within it, and the value of the system is in combining them.

@us/tomorrow-s8/66308.purpose: A Tomorrow.io microwave sounder in a mid-inclination plane, launched as a pair with S9. Tomorrow.io sells weather intelligence rather than raw radiances, and its customer list includes the US Air Force alongside commercial operators; the sounder data feeds both physical assimilation and the training and initialisation of the company's machine-learning forecast models. That dual use is the emerging pattern in commercial METOC data.

@us/tomorrow-s9/66309.purpose: The ninth Tomorrow.io microwave sounder, flown with S8. The instrument line descends directly from NASA's TROPICS demonstration, which showed that a CubeSat-class radiometer could produce tropical cyclone soundings of operational quality. Tomorrow.io enlarged the design from 3U to 6U specifically to add better calibration targets and more stable receiver electronics, the difference between a science demonstration and a sensor whose radiances a model will accept.

@us/tracers-1/64870.purpose: TRACERS 1 is one of two identical NASA spacecraft that fly in tandem, seconds to a couple of minutes apart, through the northern polar cusp — the funnel in Earth's magnetic field where solar wind particles reach the upper atmosphere most directly. Flying two in trail is the whole point: it separates change in time from change in space, which a single pass cannot do, and so settles whether magnetic reconnection at the magnetopause runs steadily or switches on and off. Launched July 2025; science data collection under way.

@us/tracers-2/64873.purpose: TRACERS 2 is one of two identical NASA spacecraft that fly in tandem, seconds to a couple of minutes apart, through the northern polar cusp — the funnel in Earth's magnetic field where solar wind particles reach the upper atmosphere most directly. Flying two in trail is the whole point: it separates change in time from change in space, which a single pass cannot do, and so settles whether magnetic reconnection at the magnetopause runs steadily or switches on and off. Launched July 2025; science data collection under way.

@us/troop-f3/68429.purpose: TROOP-F3 is a 6U CubeSat from NearSpace Launch of Upland, Indiana, the third in a series that flies several hosted customer payloads on one small bus — a payload-hosting service rather than a single-purpose spacecraft. Its predecessor TROOP-F2 also carried a Celestis memorial capsule alongside its technical payloads. Published references do not itemise the F3 manifest, so what it is carrying on this flight is not established.

@us/tyvak-0130/48606.organization: Tyvak Nano-Satellite Systems with Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
@us/tyvak-0130/48606.purpose: GeoStare 2, a 6U CubeSat flown by Tyvak with Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, carrying two MonoTele monolithic telescopes - optics machined from a single piece of fused silica, which makes them compact and unusually resistant to launch vibration and thermal swings. The mission produced high-resolution imagery from a very small aperture package and was the third flight of the miniature telescope line, aimed at space-object observation and commercial use.

@us/und-roads-1/64535.purpose: One of two identical 3U CubeSats from the University of North Dakota's Rendezvous and Operations for Autonomous Docking and Servicing programme, the first satellites built in that state. The pair demonstrate autonomous relative navigation and docking techniques between two small spacecraft, and the programme doubles as a training facility for orbit determination and satellite operations. They carry UHF, VHF and S-band radios and offer amateur digipeater service during defined phases.

@us/und-roads-2/64549.purpose: The second of two identical 3U CubeSats from the University of North Dakota's Rendezvous and Operations for Autonomous Docking and Servicing project. The pair are to phase and close to within tens of kilometres, then demonstrate autonomous relative navigation, proximity operations and docking, while training students on a new UND ground segment doing Doppler and ranging orbit determination on UHF, VHF and S-band. When power allows they also run a 1200-baud amateur digipeater.

@us/usa-115/23712.assessedBy: Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page) and Jonathan McDowell (planet4589.org GCAT)
@us/usa-115/23712.purpose: A Milstar spacecraft: a hardened, jam-resistant military communications satellite carrying extremely-high-frequency and ultra-high-frequency links for United States strategic and tactical forces. The catalogue records only a USA designation; Gunter Krebs and Jonathan McDowell independently identify this object as the second Block I Milstar, Milstar DFS-2. Block I carries the low-data-rate payload only, and satellite-to-satellite crosslinks let it pass traffic without a ground relay. It holds a geostationary slot, so its coverage footprint does not move.

@us/usa-119/23893.purpose: This object was launched by a Titan IV from Vandenberg on a National Reconnaissance Office ocean-surveillance mission: a second-generation Parcae, or NOSS, cluster whose satellites locate ships and aircraft by triangulating their radio emissions. The catalogue records only a USA designation, and analysts disagree over which catalogued object is which.

@us/usa-134/25019.assessedBy: Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page) and Jonathan McDowell (planet4589.org GCAT)
@us/usa-134/25019.purpose: A Defense Satellite Communications System III spacecraft: the nuclear-hardened, anti-jam super-high-frequency wideband relay serving the Defense Communications System, deployed forces afloat and ashore, the White House Communications Agency and the State Department. The catalogue records only a USA designation; Gunter Krebs and Jonathan McDowell both identify this flight as DSCS III B-13. From a geostationary slot it holds a fixed footprint, and its independent SHF transponder channels let one spacecraft serve several user communities at once.

@us/usa-149/26356.assessedBy: Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page) and Jonathan McDowell (planet4589.org GCAT)
@us/usa-149/26356.purpose: A Defense Support Program satellite: the infrared missile-warning constellation now operated by the U.S. Space Force, which detects the heat of ballistic-missile and space launches, and of nuclear detonations, against the Earth below. The catalogue records only a USA designation; Gunter Krebs and Jonathan McDowell both place this object at DSP Flight 20. Its geostationary orbit gives one spacecraft an uninterrupted stare at a whole hemisphere, which is what makes launch detection within seconds possible.

@us/usa-153/26575.assessedBy: Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page) and Jonathan McDowell (planet4589.org GCAT)
@us/usa-153/26575.purpose: A Defense Satellite Communications System III spacecraft, the wideband super-high-frequency backbone of United States military long-haul communications, built to keep working through jamming and nuclear effects. The catalogue records only a USA designation; Gunter Krebs and Jonathan McDowell both identify this flight as DSCS III B-11. It sits in a geostationary slot, so terminals of any size can work it without tracking, and its selectable earth-coverage, area and spot beams let the footprint be shaped to the theatre being supported.

@us/usa-164/27168.assessedBy: Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page) and Jonathan McDowell (planet4589.org GCAT)
@us/usa-164/27168.purpose: A Milstar spacecraft: the survivable, low-probability-of-intercept satellite communications system serving the President, the Secretary of Defense and deployed United States forces. The catalogue records only a USA designation; Gunter Krebs and Jonathan McDowell both identify this object as the third Block II Milstar, DFS-5. Block II adds a medium-data-rate payload to the low-data-rate one, raising throughput far enough for imagery and bulk data. It works from a geostationary slot and crosslinks directly to the rest of the constellation.

@us/usa-176/28158.assessedBy: Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page) and Jonathan McDowell (planet4589.org GCAT)
@us/usa-176/28158.purpose: A Defense Support Program satellite: the infrared early-warning system whose sensor sweeps for the plumes of ballistic-missile and space launches and for nuclear detonations. The catalogue records only a USA designation; Gunter Krebs and Jonathan McDowell agree this is DSP Flight 22, one of the last of the twenty-three DSP satellites flown. It occupies a geostationary slot, so its view of one hemisphere is continuous - the property that makes DSP a warning sensor rather than a survey one.

@us/usa-270/41744.assessedBy: Programme and flight pair published by U.S. Air Force Space Command; the object-level split into GSSAP 3 and GSSAP 4 is assessed by Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page) and Jonathan McDowell (planet4589.org GCAT)
@us/usa-270/41744.purpose: A Geosynchronous Space Situational Awareness Program satellite - a publicly acknowledged U.S. programme. GSSAP spacecraft are manoeuvrable electro-optical inspectors that observe objects in and around the geostationary belt and feed the Space Surveillance Network as a dedicated sensor. The Air Force announced that this launch carried the third and fourth GSSAP satellites; which catalogued object is which is an analyst assessment. It works from a near-geosynchronous orbit slightly off the belt, so it drifts along the belt and can close on one target after another.

@us/usa-271/41745.assessedBy: Programme and flight pair published by U.S. Air Force Space Command; the object-level split into GSSAP 3 and GSSAP 4 is assessed by Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page) and Jonathan McDowell (planet4589.org GCAT)
@us/usa-271/41745.purpose: A Geosynchronous Space Situational Awareness Program satellite, the twin of the object launched with it. GSSAP is a publicly acknowledged U.S. programme of manoeuvrable, electro-optical inspectors that characterise objects in and near the geostationary belt and report as a dedicated Space Surveillance Network sensor. The Air Force announced the third and fourth GSSAP spacecraft on this launch; assigning the fourth to this catalogue entry is an analyst assessment. Its near-geosynchronous drift orbit lets it approach and inspect satellites on the belt above or below it.

@us/usa-283/43339.assessedBy: Programme published by U.S. Air Force Space and Missile Systems Center; object-level attribution assessed by Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page) and Jonathan McDowell (planet4589.org GCAT)
@us/usa-283/43339.purpose: Continuous Broadcast Augmenting SATCOM, a military communications relay whose stated job is to augment existing military satellite communications and broadcast military data continuously in support of senior leaders and combatant commanders. The Air Force publicly identified CBAS as a payload of the AFSPC-11 launch; the catalogue itself shows only a USA designation, and it is analysts who tie the programme to this particular object. It works from a geostationary slot, so the broadcast footprint it serves stays fixed over the same part of the Earth.

@us/usa-285/43445.purpose: An Air Force Research Laboratory subsatellite released near the geostationary belt by EAGLE, the ESPA Augmented Geosynchronous Laboratory Experiment flown on the AFSPC-11 mission. @us/usa-342/55263.purpose: Continuous Broadcast Augmenting SATCOM 2, the second satellite of a U.S. Space Force relay programme that augments existing military satellite communications and continuously broadcasts military data for senior leaders and combatant commanders. Space Systems Command publicly named CBAS-2 as the forward spacecraft on the USSF-67 Falcon Heavy launch; the catalogue itself shows only a USA designation, and analysts tie that payload to this object. It holds a geostationary slot, so the area it serves does not change.

@us/usa-485/62756.assessedBy: Jonathan McDowell (planet4589.org GCAT) and Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page)
@us/usa-485/62756.purpose: One of two classified United States government payloads carried to low Earth orbit alongside a Starlink batch, sharing that batch's low, mid-inclination delivery orbit. The catalogue records only a USA designation and no mission has been disclosed. Jonathan McDowell identifies it as a Starshield satellite operated for the National Reconnaissance Office; Gunter Krebs agrees the spacecraft is probably SpaceX-built on the Starshield bus but says its purpose has not been revealed. Treat the attribution as an open-source assessment, not a published fact.

@us/usa-486/62757.assessedBy: Jonathan McDowell (planet4589.org GCAT) and Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page)
@us/usa-486/62757.purpose: The second of two classified United States government payloads flown with a Starlink batch into a low, mid-inclination orbit. The catalogue records only a USA designation and no mission has been disclosed. Jonathan McDowell identifies it as a Starshield satellite for the National Reconnaissance Office; Gunter Krebs will say only that it is an unidentified small military satellite, probably SpaceX-built on the Starshield bus, whose purpose has not been revealed. Treat the attribution as an open-source assessment rather than an established fact.

@us/uspwsa-dragoon/64542.purpose: The prototype of T1DES, the Space Development Agency's Tranche 1 Demonstration and Experimentation System — built by York Space Systems on its LX-class platform and known by York's name, Dragoon. Its job was to show that work traditionally done from geostationary orbit can be done from low orbit instead: tactical satellite communications, advanced waveforms, and Integrated Broadcast Service delivery direct to warfighter terminals. It completed its objectives, including two-way UHF tactical communication between the satellite and ground forces, after which SDA judged the remaining eleven T1DES satellites unnecessary and began descoping the contract. Dragoon is the only one ever flown.

@us/veery-0g/66675.purpose: A precursor cubesat from Care Weather Technologies, flown on the Transporter-15 rideshare as the next step after Veery 0F in a series leading to the company's planned Veery wind-scatterometer constellation. The operational goal is a radar measurement of ocean surface wind speed from a satellite of only a few kilograms, at a revisit rate no conventional scatterometer fleet can match. The precursors qualify the antenna deployment, pointing, radio and control software the radar mission depends on.

@us/viasat-1/37843.purpose: A Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300 carrying a Ka-band spot-beam payload of about 140 Gbps, described at contract award as the world's highest capacity broadband satellite. It works from Telesat's 115 degrees West slot, with Telesat providing telemetry, tracking and control and taking the Canadian portion of the coverage. Its many narrow spot beams reuse the same frequencies across the footprint, which is what makes consumer satellite broadband economic.

@us/viasat-2/42740.purpose: A Boeing BSS-702HP Ka-band high-throughput satellite designed for about 350 Gbps - some two and a half times ViaSat-1 - and about seven times its coverage area, reaching North and Central America, the Caribbean, the busy North Atlantic air corridors and the maritime routes to Europe. On-orbit testing found an antenna deployment problem that makes some spot beams behave differently from ground test, limiting the satellite to roughly 260 Gbps.

@us/viasat-3-f1/56370.purpose: ViaSat-3 Americas, first of three satellites intended to give Viasat global Ka-band coverage, each designed for more than 1 Tbps. Boeing supplied the all-electric BSS-702MP+ bus and Viasat built the payload. It reached geostationary orbit after its Falcon Heavy launch in May 2023 but suffered a major reflector deployment anomaly; by October 2023 Viasat expected to recover less than ten percent of planned throughput and filed a 420 million dollar insurance claim. The payload itself is functional.

@us/viasat-3-f2/66454.purpose: ViaSat-3 EMEA, the second satellite of the ViaSat-3 series, covering Europe, the Middle East and Africa. Like its siblings it pairs a Boeing all-electric BSS-702MP+ bus with a Viasat-built Ka-band payload in the terabit-per-second class, using very large numbers of spot beams so capacity can be concentrated where demand actually is. It was launched by an Atlas V 551 in November 2025.

@us/viasat-3-f3/68893.purpose: ViaSat-3 APAC, the third satellite of the ViaSat-3 series, covering the Asia-Pacific region and completing Viasat's intended global Ka-band footprint. It uses the same Boeing all-electric BSS-702MP+ bus with a Viasat-built terabit-class Ka-band spot-beam payload as the other two. It was launched by a Falcon Heavy in April 2026.

@us/vigoride-3/52760.purpose: Vigoride is Momentus Space's orbital transfer vehicle: a free-flying carrier that releases customer satellites into tailored orbits and uses a water-fed microwave electrothermal thruster for its own manoeuvring. Vigoride 3 carried seven small satellites, but its solar arrays failed to deploy, leaving the vehicle short of power and unable to hold reliable two-way communications despite an FCC authorisation to try alternative frequencies. Momentus confirmed only two payload deployments; the mission was largely unsuccessful.

@us/vigoride-5/55056.purpose: The second flight of Momentus's Vigoride orbital service vehicle, a free-flying tug that deploys customer satellites and hosts payloads, driven by a microwave electrothermal thruster that uses water as propellant. On this Transporter-6 flight it hosted Caltech's space-based solar power experiment, deployed a satellite carrying the Qosmosys Zeus-1 payload, and ran the first in-space tests of the water thruster.

@us/vigoride-7/68473.purpose: Momentus' seventh Vigoride orbital service vehicle, a free-flying tug of roughly 360 kg that both dispenses customer satellites and hosts payloads on-station. It manoeuvres with a water-fed microwave electrothermal thruster, an unusual propellant choice that avoids toxic hydrazine handling. On this multi-month mission it carries about ten government and commercial payloads, including autonomous rendezvous and proximity operations demonstrations, in-space assembly hardware and onboard-computing experiments.

@us/vindler-2-1/68488.purpose: One of three Vindler 2 satellites built and operated by Muon Space on its Condor-M bus, carrying a Sierra Nevada Corporation radio-frequency collection payload. Each roughly 170 kg spacecraft detects and geolocates emitters from VHF to L-band, dark vessels running without AIS and GPS jammers among them, to a stated accuracy of about one kilometre, downlinking up to 1.5 TB per day. It is a commercial RF intelligence data source sold for national-security use.

@us/vindler-2-2/68484.purpose: One of three Vindler radio-frequency intelligence satellites launched together on Transporter-16, built by Muon Space on its Condor-M bus for Sierra Nevada Corporation. Each is about 170 kg and detects and geolocates emitters from VHF up to L-band, with a stated geolocation accuracy of about one kilometre and up to 1.5 terabytes downlinked per day. The commercial market for this is finding dark vessels that have switched off AIS, and locating GPS jammers.

@us/vindler-2-3/68486.organization: Muon Space for Sierra Nevada Corporation
@us/vindler-2-3/68486.purpose: Vindler 2.0.3 is one of three RF-sensing satellites built and operated by Muon Space on its Halo bus, carrying a payload from Sierra Nevada Corporation. It detects and geolocates emitters from VHF through L-band, placing them to within about a kilometre and downlinking as much as 1.5 terabytes a day. The advertised applications are tracking dark vessels that have switched off their AIS transponders, and finding GPS jammers — both directly relevant to maritime operations.

@us/wfov-usa-332/52940.purpose: The Wide Field of View Testbed, the risk-reduction satellite for Next-Generation OPIR, the missile-warning system succeeding SBIRS. Its L3Harris WASP sensor is a staring infrared instrument — no scanning mirror — with a six-degree field of view that holds roughly a third of the Earth's disc in view continuously, watching for the exhaust plumes of missile launches. The purpose is not to warn but to gather real space-based infrared data with which to build and validate the algorithms the operational satellites will use. Millennium Space Systems built the bus; NASA Ames managed the programme for Space Systems Command.

@us/wildblue-1/29643.purpose: An early Ka-band consumer broadband satellite on the Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300 bus, carrying 35 spot beams to serve the contiguous United States from 111.1 degrees West. The programme began as KaStar, became iSky and then WildBlue; work was suspended in 2002 for lack of funding and resumed in 2003. It used the same spot-beam approach that later high-throughput satellites scaled up.

@us/wildfire-1/57764.purpose: A Tranche 0 Transport Layer satellite of the Space Development Agency's Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture — the low-orbit mesh network built to move targeting and command data satellite-to-satellite by laser crosslink instead of routing everything through a few ground stations. WILDFIRE is Lockheed Martin Space's name for its ten Tranche 0 transport spacecraft, all flown on Terran Orbital's sub-500 kg Nebula bus. @us/wsf-m/59481.purpose: The Weather System Follow-on – Microwave, the Space Force's replacement for the passive-microwave capability the Defense Meteorological Satellite Program provided for over two decades. Its Ball-built conically scanning polarimetric radiometer runs 17 channels from 10 to 89 GHz, retrieving ocean surface vector winds and the structure used to derive tropical-cyclone intensity through cloud — the measurements METOC forecasters lose first when DMSP retires — plus sea ice, soil moisture and snow depth. A government-furnished energetic charged-particle sensor closes the third gap, low-Earth-orbit space weather.

@us/xcube-1/62400.purpose: A 6U CubeSat, arranged as two 3U halves, flown by Xplore as a prototype for a planned low-orbit hyperspectral Earth-observation constellation. Sources disagree on its provenance: one records Xplore as a US operator building the spacecraft itself, another places the company in New Brunswick, Canada with the spacecraft built by Exobotics of London. The imaging payload's detailed specifications are not publicly documented.

@us/xm-5/37185.purpose: A Space Systems/Loral SSL-1300S digital audio radio satellite ordered by XM Satellite Radio in 2005 as the ground spare for its fleet. It carries a DARS payload with two nine-metre Harris-built unfurlable reflectors and more than 18 kW of end-of-life power - enough for direct reception by small vehicle and portable radios across North America. It was launched by a Proton-M/Briz-M.

@us/xm-7/47240.purpose: SXM-7, the first of SiriusXM's third-generation S-band digital audio radio satellites, built by Maxar on the SSL-1300 bus with a large unfurlable reflector. It reached geostationary orbit successfully after its December 2020 Falcon 9 launch, but about six weeks later, during in-orbit testing, its payload failed. SiriusXM declared it a total loss in February 2021 and ordered SXM-9 as the replacement. A secondary payload continues to work for a separate service.

@us/xm-8/48838.purpose: SXM-8, the second third-generation SiriusXM digital audio radio satellite, built by Maxar on the SSL-1300 bus with an S-band payload, more than 20 kW of power and a large unfurlable antenna reflector so that subscriber radios need no dish. SXM-7 and SXM-8 were ordered together in 2016 to replace the XM-3 and XM-4 satellites; SXM-7's payload then failed in orbit, leaving SXM-8 as the first of the generation to enter service.

@us/yam-10/64580.purpose: EarthDaily 1, the first satellite of the EarthDaily Constellation, flown under Loft Orbital's YAM designation because Loft integrates, launches and operates the fleet on EarthDaily's behalf. It uses the Airbus Arrow-150 bus and carries an ABB-built multispectral imager of about 22 spectral bands at roughly 5 m resolution, designed for radiometrically consistent daily coverage rather than best-single-image quality.

@us/yam-11/68991.purpose: EarthDaily 2, one of six constellation satellites deployed on a single rideshare, the launch that took the EarthDaily fleet from a pathfinder to an operating system. Each carries the same ABB 22-band multispectral imager on an Airbus Arrow-150 bus. The design priority is calibration: consistent, comparable measurements day after day are what allow genuine change detection rather than a pretty picture.

@us/yam-12/69003.purpose: EarthDaily 3, one of the six EarthDaily Constellation satellites launched together on one rideshare. The constellation is built for daily, globally consistent measurement of planetary change, with an ABB-supplied 22-band multispectral instrument at about 5 m resolution on an Airbus Arrow-150 platform. Loft Orbital supplies the satellite, the launch and the operations as a service, EarthDaily supplies the sensor and sells the data.

@us/yam-13/68993.purpose: EarthDaily 4, one of six identical constellation satellites launched on a single flight. Twenty-two spectral bands is considerably more than a conventional commercial imager carries, and the extra bands exist so the data can be atmospherically corrected and compared reliably against yesterday's pass. The ambition is scientific-grade change detection at commercial cadence, in a sun-synchronous plane.

@us/yam-14/69008.purpose: EarthDaily 5, part of the six-satellite EarthDaily deployment flown as one rideshare. The YAM designation reflects Loft Orbital's role as satellite provider and operator rather than any difference in payload: every EarthDaily spacecraft carries the same ABB multispectral instrument on the Airbus Arrow-150 bus, and uniformity is the point when the product is a consistent daily time series.

@us/yam-15/68997.purpose: EarthDaily 6, one of the six constellation satellites launched together. Loft Orbital's business model shows here in a form worth understanding: the company will fly a single hosted payload for one customer or an entire dedicated constellation for another, using the same standardised bus and ground infrastructure, which is why one catalogue name covers both roles across the YAM series.

@us/yam-16/68992.purpose: EarthDaily 7, the last of the six EarthDaily satellites deployed on a single rideshare. It carries the constellation's standard ABB-built 22-band multispectral imager at roughly 5 m ground sampling on an Airbus Arrow-150 bus, in a sun-synchronous plane that fixes the local solar time of each pass so that scenes collected weeks apart remain directly comparable.

@us/yam-17/69884.purpose: EarthDaily 8, launched singly after the six-satellite batch that preceded it. Like the rest of the constellation it is an Airbus Arrow-150 spacecraft carrying ABB's 22-band multispectral imager, integrated, launched and operated by Loft Orbital for EarthDaily Analytics. Two further satellites were planned to complete the initial ten-spacecraft system providing daily global coverage.

@us/yam-3/48915.purpose: A Loft Orbital Yet Another Mission satellite: a standardised LeoStella bus fitted with Loft's payload hub, which supplies power, data, thermal and mechanical interfaces so unrelated customers can share one spacecraft. YAM-3's manifest was genuinely mixed, Eutelsat's ELO-2 IoT radio payload alongside the Space Development Agency's POET, the Pit Boss mission-system demonstration for DARPA's Blackjack programme, plus an RGB imaging sensor.

@us/yam-5/55076.purpose: A Loft Orbital hosted-payload satellite on the LeoStella bus. Its principal payload was MURI-FD, a longwave infrared radiometric imager from Leonardo DRS, flown with a customer-furnished flight computer, a further sensing payload, and experimental and IoT S-band payloads. The value of the model is schedule: a payload developer buys a slot on an already-procured spacecraft instead of building and licensing a satellite of their own.

@us/yam-6/59126.purpose: A Loft Orbital hosted-payload microsatellite carrying a hyperspectral imager and a multispectral imager for separate customers on one LeoStella bus. Loft used this flight to introduce what it calls the Virtual Mission: rather than flying their own hardware, a customer runs software on the spacecraft's onboard compute against another payload's data, which decouples the software mission from the hardware manifest entirely.

@us/yam-7/60504.purpose: Flown as VanZyl-1, Hydrosat's first thermal infrared satellite, and unusually for the YAM line a dedicated single-customer mission rather than a shared manifest. The roughly 83 kg spacecraft uses the LeoStella bus with Loft's payload hub. Thermal infrared measures land surface temperature, from which evapotranspiration is derived, giving crop water stress, drought onset and wildfire risk well before those appear in visible imagery.

@us/yam-8/63254.purpose: The first satellite of Loft Orbital's Longbow product line, built on the Airbus Arrow-150 bus, an upgraded version of the platform originally developed for OneWeb and flown in the hundreds. Longbow buys size, weight and power headroom for payloads too demanding for Loft's earlier microsatellites. Loft has described YAM-8 as carrying several customer and company-owned payloads but did not itemise them publicly at launch, and none are asserted here.

@us/yam-9/66694.purpose: A Loft Orbital Longbow-class satellite on the Airbus Arrow-150 bus, flown on Transporter-15. It carries Wyvern's Dragonette-005 hyperspectral camera among several customer payloads, and four networked onboard compute units so multiple customers can run inference simultaneously against sensor data in orbit. Processing on the spacecraft rather than on the ground is how these constellations cut the downlink burden and the time between collection and a usable answer.
